p.seg: I humbly believe that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs,
though beyond the reach of words and language,
must rely on means for its propagation and dissemination
before it can be illuminated.
It is like using a finger to point at the moon.
The finger and the moon
are fundamentally unrelated.
Yet by knowing where the finger points,
one knows the moon's location.
Thus, the entire Buddhist canon serves as a standard for the world,
and we still depend on it today. I, a humble monk from the mountains,
have been fortunate to encounter our sagely and enlightened era,
repeatedly granted the privilege to behold your pure radiance
and receive your verbal instructions.
The sagely words are lofty and profound, beyond ordinary comprehension.
This Way is fortunate to await its revival through such encounters.
I rejoice in this rare meeting,
and dare to express my sincere and earnest plea.
I reflect that my late teacher, the former abbot of Jìngshān, Chán Master Dàhuì,
was keenly perceptive and brilliant, directly inheriting the true transmission.
With skillful means, he enlightened later learners.
His daily teachings and essential dialogues were recorded wherever he went,
and have already been compiled into books.
There is the extensive collection in thirty volumes,
and also the recorded sayings in ten volumes.
I have respectfully transcribed them and come to the court to present them.
I humbly hope that in your leisure from myriad duties, you may condescend to peruse them. I also recall that during the Jǐngdé era of Emperor Zhēnzong,
the Transmission of the Lamp compiled by monks
was authorized for inclusion in the canon.
Now, regarding the ten volumes of my late teacher's recorded sayings that I present,
I beg your sagely compassion to follow the above precedent
and specially issue an order for them also to be entered into the canon,
thereby broadening their circulation.
This would enable later learners to partake of these teachings,
and grant my late teacher a form of immortality.
I am filled with trepidation,
awaiting your command and decision on this matter.
In the third month of the seventh year of the Qiándào era,
presented in a memorial by Yùnwén, Abbot of Jìngshān Néngrén Chán Monastery, Chán Master Huìrì.
The Dōngchán Bào'ēn Guāngxiào Chán Temple in Fúzhōu, under the directive of the Grand Councilor and Governor, respectfully received the imperial decree.
Granting ten volumes of the recorded sayings of Chán Master Dàhuì.
Ordering their placement in the renowned mountain canon.
To ensure their eternal transmission.
The abbot monk reverently had them carved as scripture blocks.
Totaling thirty scrolls.
Included in the Vairocana Great Canon.
For widespread circulation.
With this merit, devoutly praying for the boundless sacred longevity of the present emperor.
Humbly wishing the imperial domain to be secure and firm.
The royal calendar ever renewed.
The Buddha's radiance increasingly luminous.
The Dharma wheel constantly turning.
Eighth year of the Qiándào era, first month, day.
The abbot monk reverently inscribed.
The master, on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the seventh year of Shàoxīng.
Held an opening ceremony at Míngqìng Monastery in Lín'ān Prefecture.
Holding up the dedication text, he showed it to the assembly and said:
"The Grand Councilor, the Retained Commissioner,
has entered the samādhi of being skilled in all arts.
Upon the tip of a writing brush, he radiates great light.
Without moving his tongue, he has already expounded the forty-two gates of prajñāpāramitā.
Do you all believe it or not?
If you do not believe,
then let the invocator
take it out again
so that those who have not heard may hear, and those who do not believe may believe."
After the dedication was read, pointing to the Dharma seat, he addressed the assembly:
"Do you see?
It cuts off the ancient path of the buddhas;
it secretly drives away a thousand demons and a hundred monsters.
Even if it were the Lamp King of Mount Sumeru,
he must swiftly bow three times." He gave a shout.
Then ascending the seat, he took incense and said:
"This stick of incense
is reverently offered for the supreme sovereign of the northern palace,
to pray above for the myriad years of longevity of the southern mountain."
Next, taking incense, he said:
"This stick of incense
is offered for the Grand Councilor, the Retained Commissioner, and all civil and military officials, that they may eternally hold their positions of emolument."
Again taking incense, he said:
"This stick of incense—
if you look at it, your eyes will dry up;
if you smell it, your brain will split open.
Meeting the noble, its value surpasses the sahā world;
meeting the base, it is not worth a single coin.
Today, before the assembly of humans and devas,
I burn it in the incense burner,
offering it for the Great Monk, the late Chányuánwù Chán Master of Zhāojué Chán Temple in Chéngdū Prefecture,
to repay the kindness of the Dharma milk."
Then, upon the seat, the head seat struck the wooden block and said:
"O assembly of dragons and elephants of the Dharma feast,
you should contemplate the foremost meaning."
The master said:
"According to the old conventions of various places and the constant norms of past and present,

even if a thousand buddhas, world-honored ones, were to appear in succession and ascend this seat, in the end, they still could not avoid this ladle of foul water. Is there anyone who can evade it? Step forth to bear witness."
At that time, a monk came out and was about to bow.
The master said:
"Adding frost on top of snow."
Then another monk rushed forward and asked:
"Humans and devas are universally gathered; the arena for selecting buddhas is opened. How will you, Master, raise the ancestral command
when the opportunity arises?"
The master said:
"A clumsy bird flies against the wind."
The monk continued:
"Throughout the realm, there is nowhere to seek;
clearly, a single point is perfectly round in the seat."
The master said:
"In the human world, no waters fail to flow eastward."
The monk continued:
"It may be said: in the three springs, fruits fill the bodhi tree;
in one night, blossoms open, fragrance pervades the world."
The master said:
"Striking and bumping."
The monk continued:
"Numerous fragrances issue from the incense burner;
soughing, the clear breeze arises on the seat."
The master said:
"Idle talk."
The monk continued:
"How can it be helped? A thousand branches of Shàoshì flowers are just blooming;
one stream of Cáoyuán waters is even clearer."
The master raised his whisk and said:
"Which branch is this?"
The monk continued:
"One who knows the tune need not raise it repeatedly;
those who understand must be startled in the dark."
The master said:
"A sharp monk asks:
'In one question and one answer, we betray our own spirit;
in citing the ancient and the modern, we bury our ancestors.
Apart from these two paths, what is the right way?'"
The master said:
"Look with divided bodies in two places."
The monk continued:
"The two or three in the land of Táng straighten their collars with respect;
the twenty-eight in Western Heaven also raise their eyebrows in joy."
The master said:
"Heaven covers without partiality; earth supports without partiality."
The monk continued:
"Such questions and answers already involve meritorious effort.
A phrase for blessing the sage—please, Master, say it quickly."
The master said:
"Always take the sun and moon as the eyes of heaven;
point out Mount Sumeru to be the mountain of longevity."
The monk continued:
"The mountains and rivers of the state increase in majestic aura;
the plants and trees of heaven and earth all receive grace."
The master said:
"Repeating verses."
The monk continued:
"Will you permit this learner to reveal another message?"
The master said:
"I will not permit."
The monk continued:
"Then I ask the Venerable to speak."
The master said:
"Since it is not permitted, what more is there to say?"
The monk continued:
"I wish to extend the hand of Zhū Yún, who broke the balustrade,
to come as the rainmaker, Fù Yuè."
The master said:
"Only this phrase is lacking."
Then several monks vied to come forth.
The master restrained them and said:
"Suppose all the grass and trees of the great earth were ground into dust,
and each dust particle had a mouth,
and each mouth possessed the unimpeded, broad, long tongue mark,
and each tongue mark produced immeasurably different sounds,
and each sound emitted immeasurably different words,
and each word contained immeasurably different subtle meanings,
and there were as many monks as those dust particles,
each possessing such a mouth, such a tongue, such sounds, such words, and such subtle meanings,
and simultaneously they raised hundreds of thousands of difficult questions,
each question different—without needing
the Elder of Jìngshān to even cough once, they would all be answered at once.
Seizing the moment, in the midst of this, he would perform immeasurable, boundless, vast buddha-works,
each buddha-work pervading the Dharma realm.
This is called: in one hair, manifesting spiritual transformations;
all buddhas simultaneously expound the sutras.
For immeasurable eons, one cannot reach its limit.
If you go on like this,
you may have a bustling gate, that's all.
But if you view it with the true eye,
it is precisely the vast, boundless karmic consciousness with no basis to rely on.
In the ancestral school, not a bit of this is of any use.
How much more so, crafting intricate phrases and displaying verbal sharpness?
Not only does it bury the ancestral teachings from the past,
it also makes monks burst their nostrils with laughter.
Therefore, it is said: a hair's-breadth of attachment is the karmic cause for the three wretched paths;
a momentary arising of emotion is the bondage for ten thousand eons.
Holy names and ordinary labels are all empty sounds;
superior forms and inferior shapes are all illusory colors.
If you seek them, will you not be burdened?
And when you tire of them, it again becomes a great affliction.
See how the virtuous ones of old gave such instruction—
like the weapons of the state, used only when there is no alternative.
In the fundamental matter, there is not even this message.
Today, this mountain monk speaks thus,
greatly like explaining dreams to one who has never dreamed,
or gouging good flesh to create a sore. Upon reflection, I deserve a beating.
Is there now anyone who can wield the poisonous hand?
If there is, you can repay the unrepayable kindness,
and together assist the transformation of non-action.
If not, I will act contrarily—
this order is given."
Suddenly taking up his staff, he said:
"Holding Mòyé sideways, the full correct command;
throughout the peaceful world, beheading the foolish and stubborn."
He tapped the staff once.
He gave a shout. Then he brought up a story:
"Once, Attendant Wáng visited Línjì.
They went together into the monks' hall.
Attendant Wáng said:
'Are all these monks reading sutras?'
Línjì said:
'They are not reading sutras.'
Attendant Wáng said:
'Are they studying Chán?'
Línjì said:
'They are not studying Chán.'
Attendant Wáng said:
'They neither read sutras nor study Chán.
What are they doing after all?'
Línjì said:
'I am teaching them all to become buddhas and patriarchs.'
Attendant Wáng said:
'Gold dust, though precious, blinds the eye when it falls in. What about that?'
Línjì said:
'I thought you were an ordinary man.'"
The master said:
"The old man Línjì wielded a vajra king's precious sword;
his spirit surged through the cosmos,
roaming freely under heaven.
Yet casually, when this official gently pressed him,
he was seen to crumble like ice melting.
Now, tell me,
what was the strength of this official?"
Listen to a verse:
"Rare events in the world and beyond the world;
to reveal them requires one of surpassing capacity.
Simply using the hand that mends robes and blends soup,
he turns the correct Dharma wheel of the Tathāgata."
"You have been standing long, kind assembly.
I pray you take good care."
The head seat struck the wooden block again and said:
"Observe carefully the Dharma of the Dharma King;
the Dharma of the Dharma King is thus."
Entering the hall to ascend the platform.
Before this mountain monk left Quánzhōu,
I had already met all of you.
In Lín'ān Prefecture I also met all of you.
Yet when arriving at this mountain, striking the Dharma drum, sitting and standing solemnly, gazing at each other eye to eye,
why then do we not recognize one another?
Precisely because it is too clear,
it instead makes attainment slow.
Evening assembly.
The Great Way is right before your mouth.
Yet it's hard to see right before your eyes.
If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way,
it is not apart from sounds, forms, and words.
Raising the whisk, he said:
This is form.
Striking the meditation seat, he said:
This is sound.
This mountain monk is now speaking endlessly -
these are words. So which one is the true essence of the Great Way?
Shouting once, he said:
This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing;
No other sounds or forms can be shown to you.
If you understand this point, all matters cease completely;
Essence and function don't hinder whether they're divided or not.
If you divide them,
When rain falls, the ground gets wet;
When sky clears, the sun comes out.
Short months have twenty-nine days,
Long months have thirty days.
If you don't divide them,
When Vajra and earth deity rub backs - one wipe and bones appear!
He added:
The ancients said:
Only the final phrase reaches the impassable barrier.
Blocking the vital ford, neither ordinary nor holy can pass.
So what is this final phrase?
After a long pause, he said:
Don't talk in your dreams!
Slapping the meditation seat, he descended from the platform.
Entering the hall.
In former days, the venerable ancestor Yáng Qí.
Pulled the plow.
Dragged the harrow.
Displaying supernatural powers for his descendants.
Carrying water and dragging mud is quite different.
An iron for pressing clothes and a pot for boiling tea are not the same.
The Master ascended the hall and brought up [a case]:
A monk asked Lìshān,
"All forms return to emptiness.
Where does emptiness return to?"
Lìshān said,
"The tongue does not leave the mouth."
The monk asked,
"Why is it so?"
Lìshān said,
"Because inner and outer are one and the same."
The Master [Yǔzhòu] said:
"When the matter exists, the lid fits the box;
When the principle accords, arrowheads meet.
One must respond like Lìshān to be adequate.
But if it were Jìngshān, I would not say so.
If someone asked, 'All forms return to emptiness—where does emptiness return to?'
The peony blossoms reveal the Bodhisattva's face;
The palm leaves scatter like a yaksha's head.
Why is it so?
Just resolve with a willing heart,
And you will certainly not be deceived."
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
Nánquán said,
"Mǎzǔ of Jiāngxī teaches 'mind itself is Buddha'.
This old teacher does not speak thus.
'Not mind, not Buddha, not thing'—
speaking this way,
is there any fault?"
Zhàozhōu bowed and departed.
At that time, a monk followed and asked Zhàozhōu:
"You bowed and immediately left—
what was your meaning?"
Zhàozhōu said:
"You should ask the venerable."
The monk went and asked:
"What was the meaning of Shěn's departure earlier?"
Nánquán said:
"He has grasped this old monk's intention."
The Master said:
"Though these two elders skillfully wiggle fingers in their boots,
they fail to realize how ugly it appears to onlookers."
On the anniversary of Monk Yuánwù's passing.
Holding incense, he pointed to the portrait and said:
This Sichuan bumpkin,
Always loved stirring up trouble.
Diving right into bustling places,
Loathed quiet and craved action.
On this day last year, he finally returned home;
This year on that day, the path remains unchanged.
Then, turning to address the assembly, he said:
What is this path that never errs?
Do you want to understand?
Each time drinking water, each time choking;
Each piece of sandalwood, each bowl of tea.
With that, he offered the incense.
Ascending the hall.
Taking up the staff, striking it once, and shouting, he said:
"Truly pitiable indeed.
Deliberately striking and shouting wildly—
what are you doing?"
Throwing it down, he said:
"Light a fire in the cold place."
Ascending the hall.
This morning, the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Who does not gaze upon the hare in the heavens?
If not for the little Śākyamuni of the Eastern Land,
This tiger of Chángshā would have been let pass.
Ascending the hall.
The Patriarch said.
When not a single thought arises,
all dharmas are without fault.
Without fault, there are no dharmas;
without arising, there is no mind.
The capacity follows the object's extinction,
the object sinks with the capacity.
Objects exist because of the perceiving capacity,
the capacity exists because of the objects.
All the great and small Patriarchs still hold the view of doctrinal teachers.
Jìngshān, however, is not like this.
The eye cannot see itself,
the knife cannot cut itself.
Eating food relieves hunger,
drinking water quenches thirst.
Línjì and Déshān are particularly confused and mistaken,
wasting their energy applying blows and shouts.
Take away the blows, remove the shouts—
those reckless fellows,
how can they be restrained?
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
When Subhūti was sitting in meditation in a cave,
devas showered flowers in praise, and one deva exclaimed:
"Who is it that praises with a shower of flowers from the sky?"
The reply came: "I am Brahmā."
The Venerable asked:
"What is your praise for?"
The deva said:
"I revere your excellent exposition of prajñā."
The Venerable said:
"I have not spoken a single word about prajñā."
"Why then do you call it excellent exposition?"
The Master gave a shout and said:
"If at that time this shout could have been delivered,
not only would it have stopped Brahmā's mouth,
but it would also have spared Jìngshān from scrutiny two thousand years later."
The deva said:
"The Venerable does not speak,
and I do not hear.
No speaking and no hearing - this is the true exposition of prajñā."
The Master gave another shout and said:
"If at that time this shout could have been delivered,
not only would it have stopped Subhūti's mouth,
but it would also have spared Jìngshān from scrutiny two thousand years later."
Now tell me:
Does Jìngshān still have any point that might be scrutinized by others?
He said himself:
"What point is there that could be scrutinized?"
I shouldn't have said so much.
Ascending the hall.
A clay ox at the bottom of the water chews on raw iron.
Jiāo Fàn Bōtí bites his tongue.
The sea god angrily wields a coral whip.
The king of Mount Xūmí feels excruciating pain.
Striking the meditation seat, he descends from it.
Ascending the hall.
Piercing the azure heavens, a pine stands a thousand feet tall.
Severing the mundane world, a single stream of water flows.
Unaware of the original true countenance,
One might mistake it for a poem inscribed by Dé Qiáo.
The magistrate of Lín'ān County stated:
He ascended the platform at Hǎihuì Temple.
The Master held up the dedication text and showed the assembly, saying:
"Before the literary brilliance is revealed, the message is already exposed.
Once the literary brilliance is revealed, it is hard to cover up.
Since it cannot be covered up,
it still requires proclamation."
Lǎng Xuān read it aloud once. After the dedication was read,
the Master looked around at the great assembly and said:
"The magistrate scholar has already expounded the ultimate truth for all of you.
Is there anyone whose eyes are opened and mind awakened?
If so, please,
you may disperse right now.
If not,
Jìngshān will instead speak empty words from the abbot's chair."
Then he ascended the seat and offered incense.
After praying for the emperor, he again offered incense, saying:
"This single stick of incense,
even the Buddhas do not know it,
spirits and demons cannot fathom it.
It is not born of heaven and earth,
nor is it obtained naturally.
The other day in the city, I already brought it forth.
Today, humans and gods are universally gathered, the fourfold assembly has all arrived.
Among them, there may be those who do not yet know its essence—
I cannot avoid explaining it clearly again."
Then he burned it and took his seat.
A monk asked:
"The breeze of Yáo eternally fans,
the Bodhisattva manifests in the body of an official.
The Buddha sun is brilliantly bright,
the old man Lú sings the melody of Shàolín.
Praying for the emperor and opening the hall, we wish to hear the essential Dharma."
The Master said:
"Startling heaven and shaking earth."
The monk continued:
"Relying on the Master's single drop of Cáoxī water,
may it become a downpour over the four seas to repay our emperor."
The Master said:
"A single wild goose first returns; autumn fills the four seas."
The monk continued:
"The golden wheel governs the three-thousandfold world,
the jade calendar extends for a million springs."
The Master said:
"Who would not wish for this?"
Another question:
"Sānshèng said,
'When I meet someone, I come forth;
having come forth, I do not act for others.'
What is the meaning?"
The Master said:
"Killing without using a knife."
The monk continued:
"Xìnghuà said, 'When I meet someone, I do not come forth;
having come forth, I then act for others.'
What about this?"
The Master said:
"Enlivening others—why necessarily a sword?"
The monk continued:
"Right at the moment of coming forth and not yet coming forth, how is it?"
The Master said:
"A lock without a key shakes at both ends."
The monk continued:
"I shall specifically go forth to spread it."
The Master said:
"Jìngshān is defeated today." Then he said:
"The ultimate truth of the Buddhadharma is not in questions and answers.
Even if questions arise like clouds of Pǔhuì,
and answers flow like Pǔxián's vase pouring out,
if one does not recognize the essential wonder,
it only becomes theatrical talk.
What benefit does it have for the Way?
Speaking according to reality,
it's all madness running outside.
Therefore, the Great Awakened World-Honored One appeared in the world for the cause of the one great matter.
Using various subtle, skillful means, he accomplished sentient beings,
opening, showing, awakening, and entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
Rising from the Bodhi tree, he went to the Deer Park,
first turning the Dharma wheel of the four truths for Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
For forty-nine years, over three hundred and sixty assemblies,
according to the suitable capacities of sentient beings' roots, he sequentially expounded,
enabling each to hear the Dharma, understand, awaken, and transcend birth and death.
Finally, approaching parinirvāṇa,
before an assembly of millions of humans and gods,
he held up a flower and universally showed it.
Only the golden-colored one broke into a slight smile.
Then he said:
'I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa,
which I entrust to you.'
Since then, in the West twenty-eight, in the East twenty-three,
all the old venerables under heaven have transmitted mind to mind, continuing unbroken.
If one does not recognize the essential wonder,
but constantly drowns in knowledge and views, racing with words,
how could the treasury of the true Dharma eye have been transmitted to this day?
Reaching here, one must be an extraordinary person who seeks not the sages nor values his own spirit, able to shoulder this great matter.
So, who is this extraordinary person?
Don't you recall formerly, when the Great Master Mǎ of Jiāngxī
sent Zhìcáng of the Western Hall
to deliver a letter to National Preceptor Yī of Jìngshān?
National Preceptor Yī opened the envelope and saw a circle.
Then, taking a brush, facing Zhìcáng,
he placed a dot inside the circle.
Zhìcáng was at a loss.
Isn't this a message beyond the ordinary?
If you discuss it as beyond the ordinary,
it is not so.
How do you all discern it?
How do you apply it in daily life?
Earlier, in the magistrate scholar's dedication, it was said:
'Mǎ's circular symbol remotely conveyed the pure regulations over a thousand miles;
Qīn's sharp response punctured the confusion of the assembly at once.'
Since the assembly's confusion was punctured,
then everyone's great matter at the base is thoroughly clear.
Since the great matter is clear,
then in the twelve periods, every turn and bow, snap of fingers and cough, is none other than the Buddha's wondrous function.
Since it is the Buddha's wondrous function,
it is not obtained from others.
Since it is not obtained from others,
it is also not in one's own person.
Since it is not in one's own person,
then internally not released, externally not admitted.
Since externally not admitted, then external conditions cease.
Internally not released,
then the inner mind does not pant.
Since the inner mind does not pant and external conditions cease,
then all wisdom is unobstructed.
Since there is no obstruction,
then the wisdom of all wisdoms is pure,
without duality, without twofoldness,
without differentiation, without interruption.
Right at such a time,
it is not worldly dharmas,
nor is it beyond-worldly dharmas.
Pulling Zhànbō Kingdom to wrestle with Xīnluó Kingdom—
how could this be extra?
Even so,
there is still further matter.
I dare ask all of you:
Just why did National Preceptor Zhōng say,
'Preceptor Qīn is still confused by Mǎ'?
Is there anyone now who can settle this?
If you can settle it,
I acknowledge all of you
as extraordinary persons.
If not,
Jìngshān will close the case according to the record."
After a long pause, he said:
"At home, one only says being a guest is easy; facing the net, one realizes catching fish is hard."
Ascending the hall.
A monk asked,
"At the assembly on Língshān, Jiāshè personally heard;
Before Shǎoshì Peak, Shénguāng obtained the marrow.
Now beneath this seat, who is the one who understands the music?"
The master said,
"Tear apart the tongue."
The monk continued,
"It may be said, in Biàn's arena there are many great uncut gems;
At Mèngcháng's gate, there are plenty of distinguished guests."
The master said,
"No need to bring out rubble."
The monk continued,
"But how can one deny that before the sharp edge there is difference,
In the phrases there is no partiality?"
The master said,
"Who is the one who understands the music?"
The monk continued,
"Before Shǎoshì Cliff, a golden phoenix dances;
On Jìngshān Peak's summit, a jade rooster crows."
The master said,
"A double-layered public case."
A question:
"Bodhidharma came from the west, solely transmitting the mind seal;
Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing nature and becoming a Buddha.
Just as Déshān upon entering the gate immediately used the stick,
Línjì upon entering the gate immediately shouted—unclear whether they are the same or different?"
The master made a shushing sound.
The monk continued,
"If so, then without leaving the present place, constantly serene;
Seeking, one knows you cannot be found."
The master said,
"Where fish swim, the water is turbid."
The monk continued,
"But how about stepping on a steelyard weight, hard as iron?"
The master said,
"Cannot be lured." The monk continued,
"In every instance where guidance is given,
Look carefully and well."
The master said,
"I spare you thirty blows."
Then he said,
"No need to arrange, absolutely do not contrive.
Contriving and arranging, without a rope, you bind yourself.
Without arranging, without contriving, Shàncái snaps his fingers and ascends the tower.
Mímó sets down the fork in his hand;
Pǔhuà enters the market shaking his bell."
The master ascended the hall and cited Pánshān's saying:
"The mind-moon, solitary and round, its light engulfs all phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects vanish, what thing remains?"
Dòngshān said:
"Before light and objects vanish, what thing is it?"
The master said:
"A white egret descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow;
a yellow oriole perches on the branch—a single spray of blossoms."
The Master ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"When Guīyǎng met, they planted the spade and folded their hands.
What is the meaning?"
The Master said,
"Two eyes facing two eyes."
The monk continued,
"Few know the music on the stringless lute;
When father and son play, the melody is sublime."
The Master said,
"You tell me,
Is it in planting the spade or in folding the hands?"
The monk responded,
"From the tip of the pole, the silk thread follows the Master's handling;
Without touching the clear waves, the meaning is naturally distinct."
The Master said,
"So it goes like this again."
Then he said,
"With phrases or without phrases, like a vine clinging to a tree;
The blue-eyed foreigner doesn't know where it falls.
Now tell me,
Where does it fall?"
Suddenly taking up his staff, he addressed the assembly, saying,
"Look, look!
It comes straight down!"
Urgently fixing their eyes to see, he threw down the staff.
Returned from leading the congregation.
Ascending the hall, he recounted how the Fifth Patriarch returned from leading the congregation.
He addressed the assembly, saying:
"After half a month away with the congregation,
my eyes could not see my nostrils.
I lost the Patriarch's Chan,
but picked up an antique.
Now tell me,
where should it be placed?
One portion I offer to Śākyamuni Buddha,
one portion I offer to the Prabhūtaratna Stupa."
Jìngshān's dharma descendant has been away with the congregation for over eighty days.
His nostrils have constantly been visible to his eyes,
nor is there any Patriarch's Chan to lose,
nor has he picked up any antique.
Since there is no antique, there is nothing to offer to Śākyamuni Buddha,
nor anything to offer to the Prabhūtaratna Stupa.
After all, what has he gained?
The night is still, the water cold—the fish do not bite;
the boat returns empty, laden only with moonlight.
Ascending the hall.
Last year on the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month, there was such news.
This year on the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month, there is no such news.
Having such news
is a matter within your domain.
Jìngshān has no part in it.
Lacking such news
is a matter within Jìngshān's domain.
You all have no share in it.
If someone were to ask,
"Jìngshān, what exactly is this news?"
Suddenly raising his staff, he said:
"Do not move it.
If you move it, I will break your donkey's back."
Throwing down the staff, he descended from the seat.
On New Year's Day, ascending the platform.
Taking up the staff and writing in the air.
Making the gesture of writing characters, saying:
"On this first morning, taking up the brush, all matters are auspicious.
Timely receiving blessings, every celebration is fitting.
If treated as worldly conventions spreading on level ground,
one stumbles; moreover, in discussing the Buddha Dharma, eyebrows and beard fall off."
Planting the staff firmly and descending the seat.
Ascending the hall.
Buying iron, one obtains true gold.
Praying for rain, one receives auspicious snow.
The five peaks carved from jade.
A thousand trees adorned with silver blossoms.
The Dragon King bestows blessings.
Samantabhadra reveals clumsiness.
The secret gate of the Tathāgatas of the three periods.
Today, all is divulged at once.
Even so, there is one doubtful point here.
Pray tell,
what is the doubt?
Fear that after sunrise, there will be a moment of delay.
Ascending the hall.
On the Lantern Festival, all rejoice together.
Everywhere shines the inexhaustible lamp.
The light flashes, breaking the face of intense heat.
The night god suddenly suffers from a cold headache. Investigate.
The Master ascended the hall and brought up a case: A monk asked Changsha,
"How can one turn mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into oneself?"
Changsha said,
"How can one turn oneself back into mountains, rivers, and the great earth?"
The Master said,
"Turning mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into oneself is easy;
turning oneself back into mountains, rivers, and the great earth is difficult.
If anyone can speak the phrase of neither difficulty nor ease,
come before Jìngshān and receive a stick from my hand."
Ascending the hall.
In mid-spring's second month, the long rain refuses to clear.
Yúnmén's one thrust—virtue finds no neighbor.
He then gazed upon the assembly and said:
Thrust.
Again he said:
Shame and dread are killing.
Layman Bùdòng arrived.
The Master ascended the platform.
A monk asked,
"Jìngshān has deployed the dragon-snake battle formation.
The Layman comes with a single horse and lone spear.
At such a moment, how do you meet?"
The Master said,
"This old monk beats the retreat drum."
The monk continued,
"An old tiger
encounters a double-fanged beast."
The Master said,
"Do you still hear the thunder's roar?"
The monk advanced,
"Only because this student is accustomed to it."
The Master said,
"Don't feign clarity."
The monk continued,
"Yet I request the Venerable to speak."
The Master said,
"If I speak,
you'll be shattered into fragments."
The monk advanced,
"Then I'll rejoice and depart this life."
The Master made a "xū xū" sound and said,
"Eyes empty, the cosmos holds nothing at all;
Sitting grandly before the hall, who dares peek?
Choosing Buddhas and selecting officials—both finished;
Walking the same path hand in hand, yet not returning together."
He then asked the assembly,
"Since we walk the same path and join hands,
why don't we return together?
Don't mistake the crane's cry for an oriole's song."
He further cited: Official Lù Gèng asked Nánquán,
"Master Zhào was quite remarkable,
explaining that heaven, earth and I share the same root, all things and I are one body."
Nánquán then pointed to flowers in the courtyard and told the official,
"People today see this cluster of flowers
as if in a dream."
The Master said,
"This kōan has circulated through the monasteries for nearly three hundred years.
During this time, countless wise teachers have appeared in the world,
yet not one has ever clearly adjudicated it for him.
Today Jìngshān will settle it for him.
If viewed from the perspective of principle,
not only could Nánquán not deceive Lù Gèng in the slightest,
he hadn't even touched a single hair at his feet.
If viewed from the perspective of phenomena,
not only could Lù Gèng not deceive Nánquán in the slightest,
he hadn't even dreamed of
his sweaty odor.
Should someone come forth and say,
'Big or small, Jìngshān speaks of principle and phenomena,'
then tell him,
'Just try to grasp it through principle and phenomena.'"
Ascending the hall.
One does not make a pair.
Two does not make a couple.
Shouting once, saying:
What is this?
The sword is named Jùquē, the pearl is called Yèguāng.
Ascending the hall.
A monk asked,
"Old Dōngshān also raised it thus,
Old Yuánwù also raised it thus.
I wonder how you, Reverend, would raise it?"
The master said,
"One hand does not clap alone;
with two hands, they clap loudly."
The monk advanced, saying,
"Gold does not exchange for gold;
water does not wash water."
The master said,
"You've missed it and don't even know."
The monk advanced, saying,
"Above is heaven, below is earth—
what exactly has been missed?"
The master said,
"Gold does not exchange for gold;
water does not wash water—do you hear?"
The monk advanced, saying,
"Directly coming down, one must urgently fix their gaze."
The master said,
"Still, you cannot leap out." Then he raised
a monk's question to Tóuzǐ:
"Within the entire Buddhist canon, is there anything extraordinary?"
Tóuzǐ said,
"It expounds the great canon."
Another old master said,
"It enters into the great canon."
The master said,
"Expounding out and entering in—these two elders certainly did so.
But as for extraordinary matters,
even after three lifetimes and sixty kalpas, they have not yet dreamed of them."
On the anniversary of Chán Master Wúshàng's passing, he ascended the platform.
Just before the drum was struck,
Chán Master Wúshàng had already immersed himself in mud and water for everyone,
entangling them with many complications.
Jìngshān should not add more mud to the earth.
Then he descended from the seat.
The master ascended the hall and cited Yǒngjiǎ's words:
"The river moon shines, the pine wind blows.
What is to be done throughout the long night, the clear evening?
The Buddha-nature is the precept pearl, the mind-seal.
Mist, dew, clouds, and rosy dawn are the robe upon the body."
The master said:
"This worthy deserves thirty blows.
Now tell me,
wherein lies the fault?
He should not have stolen
the eternal property and put it under his robe and bowl."
The Master ascended the hall and cited the teaching:
"One should thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand without giving rise to dharma characteristics."
The Master raised his whisk and said:
"This is Jìngshān's whisk."
"What do you call dharma characteristics?"
"Since dharma characteristics cannot be obtained,"
"Then what is there to know? What is there to see?"
"What is there to believe?"
"What is there to understand?"
Again raising it, he said:
"This is dharma characteristics."
"Then what do you call a whisk?"
"Since the whisk cannot be obtained,"
"Thus knowing,"
"Thus seeing,"
"Thus believing and understanding,"
"What fault is there in this?"
"At just such a moment, how would you speak the turning phrase?"
"A thousand layers, a hundred coils - no mutual turning."
"Everyone, in stillness - svāhā!"
Ascending the hall.
Today marks yet another first of April.
That matter remains utterly without news.
The monk's robe has long been damp,
but joyfully, the sun rises in the east.
Meditate.
Bathing the Buddha, ascending the hall.
This very morning is the eighth of the fourth month.
In King Śuddhodana's palace, Siddhārtha was born.
Nine dragons spitting water descend from beyond the heavens,
Seven lotuses supporting his feet emerge from the earth.
Pointing to his chest and ribs, he alone claims supremacy,
Opening his mouth wide, he boasts of his own merits.
Altogether dwelling in the world for over seventy years,
Forty-nine years filled with sorrow and distress.
Fortunately, there was the old lame master of Yúnmén,
Who at that time wanted to strike him dead with a single blow.
Everyone says they repay the Buddha's kindness,
Offering this profound heart to the dust-like realms.
Only Jìngshān is not like this.
Since it's not so, what should be done?
Descending the seat.
Together proceed to the hall,
To explain it clearly for all of you.
He ascended the hall.
Lifting his staff and striking it once, he called out to the assembly, saying:
"Do you hear?"
Then raising it again, he said:
"Guānshìyīn Púsà has arrived, right here on Jìngshān's staff's tip.
Muttering with his mouth, he speaks:
'All conditioned things are impermanent, subject to birth and death.
When birth and death are extinguished, tranquil extinction appears before you.'
Lifting Sumeru in the palm of his hand,
Swinging on a swing through the eye of a needle.
Even if you can see through it like this thoroughly,
It still falls short by a hundred and eight thousand compared to this staff.
Now tell me,
What is so extraordinary about Jìngshān's staff?"
Throwing it down, he said:
"Not worth half a cent."
Ascending the hall.
Jìngshān has not an inch of land or manor fields.
This summer, as appropriate, we gather with the assembly.
Too idle to discuss the Way, too lazy to speak of Chán.
The staff I carry brings forth each one's perfection.
There's no need to calm the mind to eliminate delusive thoughts.
Everyone, after eating, just sleep soundly.
Sleeping soundly is fine,
but what if in a dream someone demands payment for the meal?
Vaguely like a melody, just when it becomes worth hearing,
it is blown by the wind into another tune.
The master ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"The Dharma body has three kinds of sickness and two kinds of light.
I won't ask about the light.
I wonder, does the Dharma body still possess the four great elements?"
The master said, "It does."
The monk continued,
"What is the Dharma body?"
The master said,
"Earth, water, fire, wind."
The monk continued,
"What are the four great elements?"
The master said, "You lacquer bucket, so slow!"
The monk continued,
"Beyond the Dharma body, is there still anything further?"
The master said,
"Just understand what is below."
Then he brought up a monk asking Zhàozhōu,
"What is the person who has come out?"
Zhàozhōu said,
"All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The master said,
"What a Zhàozhōu,
originally so timid!"
"If someone asked Jìngshān,
'What is the person who has come out?'
I would tell him,
'Mud pigs and mangy dogs.'
If he then said,
'Jìngshān's tongue is so free and unrestrained,'
I would know you are a lacquer bucket."
The Master ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"When all activities cease and one sits alone in the great square,
this is still a matter of the lower level.
What is the matter of the upper level?"
The Master said,
"One should not speak of dreams before a fool."
The monk continued,
"The old monk's three inches are very secret."
The Master said,
"It is difficult to deceive the eyes of the multitude."
The monk continued,
"Just as when a monk asked Dòngshān, 'What is Buddha?'
He said, 'Three pounds of flax.' How about that?"
The Master said,
"The great roc spreads its wings, covering the ten continents;
The creatures by the fence chirp in vain."
Then he said,
"Yesterday was clear, today it rains.
The timing does not correspond.
Look into it three days later."
Striking the meditation seat, he descended.
Ascending the hall.
A monk asked,
"When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed;
when thought changes, the essence differs.
Before emotion arises, from where does the obstruction come?"
The master said,
"So it turns out to be a rice bag."
The monk pressed further,
"I do not understand the intended meaning."
The master said, "Obstruction."
Then, raising his staff, he cited
Sānshèng's words:
"When I meet someone, I emerge;
emerging, I do not act for others."
Tapping once, he said,
"The thief's body is already exposed—letting it pass is unacceptable."
Xīnghuà, upon hearing this, said,
"When I meet someone, I do not emerge;
emerging, I act for others."
Tapping once again, he said,
"The thief's body is already exposed—it must not be let pass."
Generally, when a patriarch decides right and wrong,
he must open people's eyes;
he cannot blindly apply fetters and strikes.
Now, tell me,
what fault do these two old men have?
Throwing it down, he said,
"Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish, but monks are hard to deceive."
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
A monk asked Dòngshān,
"When cold and heat arrive, how does one avoid them?"
Shān said,
"Why not go to the place without cold or heat?"
The monk said,
"What is the place without cold or heat?"
Shān said,
"When cold, it utterly freezes the Ācārya;
when hot, it utterly burns the Ācārya."
Also, a monk asked an old master,
"The season is so hot like this,
where should one go to avoid it?"
The master said,
"Go avoid it within the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnace coals."
The monk said,
"How can one avoid it within the cauldrons of boiling water and furnace coals?"
The master said,
"The multitude of sufferings cannot reach there."
The Teacher said,
"These two old masters—
one extends a helping hand within cold and heat,
one extends a helping hand outside cold and heat.
The one extending a hand within cold and heat does not see the characteristics of cold and heat.
The one extending a hand outside cold and heat—
their entire body is cold and heat.
Jìngshān speaking like this,
can all of you discern it clearly?
If you can discern it clearly,
Nántiāntái and Běiwǔtái are yours.
If you cannot discern it clearly,
today's heat is just like yesterday's."
The master ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"The teachings say:
Every speck of dust preaches, every land preaches, without interruption.
I wonder what is used as the tongue?"
The master slapped the right corner of the meditation seat once.
The monk continued,
"The World-Honored One speaks without speaking,
and Mahākāśyapa hears without hearing."
The master slapped the left corner of the meditation seat once.
The monk said, "Now I know today's instruction was not in vain."
The master said,
"You recognize what's good and bad!"
Then he brought up how Zhàozhōu asked Nánquán,
"Where does the person who knows 'It' go?"
Nánquán said,
"He goes to become a water buffalo at the patron's home in front of the mountain."
Zhàozhōu said,
"Thank you, Teacher, for your answer."
Nánquán said,
"Last night at midnight, the moonlight reached the window."
Yúnfēng commented,
"If Nánquán hadn't added those last words,
he would have nearly had Càizhōu broken through."
The master said,
"Old man Yúnfēng has lost one eye!
He doesn't realize that precisely because of those last words,
Càizhōu was broken through right then and there."
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
Xìnghuà said to Kèbīn, the rector,
"You will soon become a guiding teacher."
Kèbīn said,
"I won't join this community."
Xìnghuà said,
"Whether you understand or not, you won't join?"
"Whether you understand or not, you won't join?"
Kèbīn said,
"It's not like that at all."
Xìnghuà then struck him, saying:
"Kèbīn the rector has lost the Dharma combat."
"He is fined five strings of cash,"
"and must provide a meal for the assembly."
The next day, Xìnghuà personally struck the wooden gavel and declared:
"Kèbīn the rector has lost the Dharma combat."
"He is fined five strings of cash,"
"must provide a meal for the assembly,"
"and must leave the monastery."
Yúnjū Shùn the venerable said:
"Fine gold from a great furnace should not change color."
"However, Xìnghuà's decree is too severe."
"Not only Kèbīn the rector - even others would find it hard to bear."
"But nowadays, those ordinary fellows,"
"how long would it take them to turn their faces around?"
The Master said:
"Yúnjū speaking like this"
"unavoidably twists the straight and makes it crooked."
"Jìngshān, however, says otherwise:"
"To become Línjì's brilliant descendants,"
"one must indeed turn one's face around."
Entering the hall.
A monk asked:
Línjì said:
"After my death, do not extinguish my treasury of the true dharma eye."
Sānshèng came forward and said:
"Who would dare extinguish the venerable's treasury of the true dharma eye?"
"What is the treasury of the true dharma eye?"
The master said:
"Yànshēn, you thieving rascal!"
"How could you comprehend the treasury of the true dharma eye?"
The monk continued:
"Línjì said:"
"If someone asks you, what would you do?"
Sānshèng then shouted.
Línjì said:
"Who would have known my treasury of the true dharma eye"
"would be extinguished by this blind donkey!"
"What is the meaning of this?"
The master said:
"Profit moves even the noble man."
Then he cited:
The king of Jibì country raised his sword and asked尊者 Shīzǐ:
"Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates?"
尊者 said:
"I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates."
The king said:
"Have you transcended life and death?"
尊者 said:
"I have already transcended life and death."
The king said:
"Can you give me your head?"尊者 said:
"The body is not mine to possess,"
"how much less the head!"
The king then beheaded him.
White milk spurted over ten feet high,
and the king's arm fell off by itself.
Xuědòu said:
"A true master of kings, naturally he remains."
Huánglóng Xīn和尚 said:
"Huánglóng wants to ask Xuědòu:"
"Since he was a true master of kings,"
"why did his arm fall off?"
The master said:
"Mèng Bāláng fellow!"
"Again going on like that."
The hall raised the saying of Elder Bái Yúnduān: If one truly breaks into a sweat once,
then upon a single blade of grass
appear jade towers and palaces.
If one has not truly broken into a sweat once,
even if there are jade towers and palaces,
they will be covered by a single blade of grass.
The Master said:
"Jade towers and palaces appearing on a single blade of grass—
this can certainly be believed.
Jade towers and palaces being covered by a single blade of grass—
do not be deceived by its heat."
Jìngshān speaks thus
for those who have already broken into a sweat once.
As for those who have not yet broken into a sweat once,
they absolutely must not harbor doubts.
Ascending the hall on the Tiānshēn Festival.
I bow my head to the one who can deliver all worlds.
An immeasurable and supremely wondrous accumulation of merit and virtue.
The golden wheel monarch rules over the four continents.
Universally bestowing peace and happiness upon all living beings.
Is there anyone who knows gratitude and repays kindness?
After a long pause, he said:
Throughout the three hundred and sixty days of the year,
Only this day is the most auspicious.
The Master ascended the hall and cited [the case]:
Bǎilíng asked Layman Páng,
"Have you ever shared with others the essential phrase you gained from Shítóu?"
The Layman said,
"I have indeed shared it with someone."
Bǎilíng asked,
"With whom did you share it?"
The Layman pointed to his own chest and said,
"With Layman Páng."
Bǎilíng said,
"Even the wondrous virtue of Śāriputra and Subhūti
could not praise this enough."
Layman Páng then asked Bǎilíng,
"Venerable, have you ever shared with others the essential phrase you gained from Shítóu?"
Bǎilíng said,
"I have indeed shared it with someone."
The Layman asked,
"With whom did you share it?"
Bǎilíng put on his bamboo hat and immediately left.
The Master said,
"This dialogue—
had it not been for Layman Páng,
he might almost have shared it with the wrong person.
Nevertheless,
Bǎilíng was outdone by Layman Páng in this move.
Why?
If at that moment he hadn't used that tattered hat to cover his skull,
what face would he have had to see Layman Páng?"
Ascending the hall.
When deluded thoughts arise, birth and death continue.
When deluded thoughts cease, birth and death are severed.
Where birth and death are severed, nirvana is empty.
Where nirvana is empty, it is like dust in the eye.
Since nirvana is empty,
what can be called dust in the eye?
White clouds may come to the green peaks,
but the bright moon is hard to bring down from the blue sky.
The Master ascended the hall and cited [the story]:
Wúzhù went to Mount Wǔtái to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī asked,
"Virtuous one, from which direction have you come?"
Wúzhù said,
"From the south."
Mañjuśrī said,
"How is the Buddha-Dharma maintained in the south?"
Wúzhù said,
"In this degenerate age, few bhikṣus uphold the precepts."
Mañjuśrī said,
"How many are the assembly?"
Wúzhù said,
"Sometimes three hundred, sometimes five hundred."
Wúzhù then asked,
"Reverend, how is the Buddha-Dharma maintained here?"
Mañjuśrī said,
"Ordinary people and saints dwell together, dragons and snakes intermingle."
Wúzhù said,
"How many are the assembly?"
Mañjuśrī said,
"Three times three in front, three times three behind." The Master said,
"If Jìngshān had been there at that time,
he would have immediately told him,
'Reverend, maintaining it like this
is extremely difficult.'"
Ascending the hall.
Taking up the staff, striking it once, and shouting, he said:
Déshān's stick, Línjì's shout.
Today for you, I take them up again.
How high is heaven, how vast is earth?
Cease adding clutter atop the dung heap.
Change your bones, wash your guts.
Jìngshān retreats three steps,
Allowing you all to deliberate.
So how will you deliberate?
Throwing down the staff and shouting once, he said:
Rouge and powder easily make a fair maiden,
Without money, it's hard to be a fine young man.
The Master ascended the hall.
A monk asked:
"Xuěfēng visited Tóuzǐ three times and Dòngshān nine times.
Why did he attain enlightenment at Áo Mountain?"
The Master said:
"Selling Yángzhōu goods in one's own house."
The monk continued:
"Later when dwelling in a hermitage,
a monk knocked at the door.
Xuěfēng thrust out his body and said:
'What is it?'
The monk also said:
'What is it?'
Is there any superiority or inferiority between them?"
The Master said:
"If superior, both are superior.
If inferior, both are inferior."
The monk continued:
"Why did Xuěfēng lower his head and return to the hermitage?"
The Master said:
"It puzzles everyone under heaven."
The monk continued:
"The monk reported this to Yántóu.
Yántóu said:
'If I had told him the final word at that time,
no one under heaven could have done anything to old Xuě.'
What is the final word?"
The Master said:
"If you don't share the same bed,
how would you know the quilt is worn through?"
The monk continued:
"Yántóu said:
'Xuěfēng and I were born of the same branch,
but we won't die of the same branch.
If you want to know the final word,
this is it.'
What is the meaning?"
The Master said:
"To kill people, you need a killing knife.
To enliven people, you need an enlivening sword."
Then he said:
"An ancient worthy said:
'Green vines twining,
climb straight to the top of cold pines.
White clouds drifting lightly,
appear and disappear within the great emptiness.'
All dharmas are originally tranquil,
only people themselves create disturbance."
Also, the teachings say:
"Ordinary people perceive all dharmas but follow forms,
not understanding that dharmas are formless.
Therefore they don't see the Buddha."
Then raising his whisk, he said:
"This is form.
That is formless.
All the myriad phenomena presently before our eyes,
all are dharmas.
When have they ever been disturbed?
Since they've never been disturbed,
what thing is there that follows forms?"
Again raising his whisk, he said:
"This is formless.
Then what understanding is there?
Since there's nothing to understand,
where do you see the Buddha?
Tell me, are the ancient worthy's words correct,
or are the teachings' words correct?
If both are correct,
what exactly are they?
If you can analyze this clearly here,
then Shakyamuni doesn't come before Maitreya.
Although this is so,
you still can't avoid having your nostrils pierced by this mountain monk's whisk."
Again raising his whisk, he said:
"Following forms -
your nostrils are pierced by the whisk.
Not following forms -
your nostrils are pierced by the whisk.
Seeing the Buddha - your nostrils are pierced by the whisk.
Not seeing the Buddha - your nostrils are pierced by the whisk."
Then looking around at the assembly, he said:
"So how can you avoid this fault?
After all, water must return to the sea;
in the end, clouds surely seek the mountains."
He struck the meditation seat and descended.
The Master ascended the hall and cited [a case]:
A monk asked Mǐhú,
"Since ancient times, have the superior sages
attained the true principle or not?"
Hú said, "They attained it."
The monk asked,
"Then as for the true principle,
how did they attain it?"
Hú said,
"Back then, when Huò Guāng sold the fake silver city to the Shànyú with a contract,
who was it that made [the deal]?"
The monk was speechless.
The Master said,
"If Jìngshān had been that monk at the time,
he would have offered a turning phrase
to shut this old man's mouth.
Now, what phrase should be offered?"
After a long pause, he said,
"If it were easily obtained,
it would be regarded as ordinary."
The assembly is called to order.
This mountain monk today has prepared congee to offer to the assembly.
After the congee, we will all go to the Dragon King Hall to chant.
After chanting, there will be a general request to send off the patron Yàn Huà to be cremated.
There are many such matters.

Before the fifteenth day,

After the fifteenth day,

Universal.

Ascending the hall.
With the arising of mind, dharmas perish.

He always passes before the Five Phoenix Tower,

It does not dwell in the present.

Entering the hall.
A monk asked:
"In Huáizhōu, oxen eat the grain.
In Yìzhōu, horses suffer bloated bellies.
Across the world, people seek a doctor,
who cauterizes the left shoulder of a pig.
Is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers,
or is it just the nature of reality?"
The master said:
"It is not the wondrous function of spiritual powers,
nor is it just the nature of reality."
The monk pressed:
"What is it, then, ultimately?"
The master said:
"An eight-foot eyebrow grows beneath the chin."
Then he said:
"The Great Way is right before your eyes,
yet before your eyes it's hard to see.
If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way,
it is not separate from sounds, forms, and words.
But if you seek the true essence through sounds, forms, and words,
it's like raking the ashes looking for a bubble.
If you seek the true essence apart from sounds, forms, and words,
it's like being in Hányuán Palace yet searching for Cháng'ān.
Not going along with any of this,
what is it, then, ultimately?
A kingfisher overturns the lotus leaves in the rain;
an egret breaks through the bamboo grove's mist."
A sermon on bathing the Buddha.
In the garden of Viran, it never arose;
Under the twin trees, how could it perish?
Seeing Gautama as neither arising nor perishing,
Is but adding another speck in the eye.
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat.
On this day, monasteries everywhere
all abide by the bodhisattva vehicle, cultivating the practice of serene extinction.
Taking the perfect enlightenment as our monastery,
body and mind dwell peacefully in the wisdom of equality.
Jìngshān, however, does otherwise.
From today onward, for ninety days,
I will join the monks in eating rice-less meals,
chewing on udumbara roots,
drinking non-wetting water,
and speaking dream-talk.
Now tell me, such cultivation as this—
compared with the summer retreats elsewhere,
how far apart are they?
After a long pause, he said:
"Dedicate this profound mind to every speck of dust in the universe,
this indeed is called repaying the Buddha's kindness."
Descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall.
When body, speech, and mind are pure,
this is called the Buddha appearing in the world.
When body, speech, and mind are impure,
this is called the Buddha's parinirvana.
I now assure you of this matter for you;
it is ultimately not false.
But then, what exactly is this matter?
And further, how does one protect and maintain it?
Haven't you seen:
A monk asked Guīzōng,
"What is the Buddha?"
Guīzōng said,
"If I tell you,
will you believe it or not?"
The monk said,
"The venerable's sincere words—
how dare I not believe?"
Guīzōng said,
"You are it."
The monk said,
"How to protect and maintain it?"
Guīzōng said,
"With a speck in the eye, phantom flowers fall wildly."
The Master said:
Guīzōng, when letting go, was too dangerous;
when reining in, was too hasty.
If that monk had at that time clapped his hands, laughed heartily for a moment,
where could old man Guīzōng have placed his face then?
I venture to ask all of you:
Now, what should be done?
One breath, unspoken, contains the image;
myriad spirits—where can they repay such selflessness?
Entering the hall.
The twenty-fifth day of the fourth month.
After long clear skies, suddenly comes rain.
The great immortal mind from India,
East and West secretly transmit.
This still belongs to seasonal conditions and causes.
It is not yet the news under the patch-robed monk's gate.
Then what exactly is the news under the patch-robed monk's gate?
After a long pause, he said:
The old tiger of the northern mountain
Has bitten to death the tiger of the southern mountain.
The master ascended the hall and cited [the case]:
When Gāotíng first called upon Déshān,
he paid his respects from across the river.
Déshān beckoned to him with his hand.
Suddenly Gāotíng attained enlightenment.
Thereupon he went straight across and left,
without even turning his head for another look.
Later he opened a monastery as Déshān's dharma successor.
The master said:
"Gāotíng going straight across and leaving—
we may allow that he was a sharp-witted monk.
But if we speak of him succeeding Déshān in the dharma,
that is still not acceptable.
Why? Because he still remains separated from Déshān by the river."
Ascending the hall.
How like a falcon soaring through the heavens.
Piercing through ten thousand layers of clouds in a single thrust.
The ancients spoke in such a manner.
Much like one with eye disease seeing flowers in the sky.
Jìngshān, however, says:
How about this—do not indulge in delusive thoughts.
Even if one penetrates through past and present,
it is still but a monkey's trick.
The Master ascended the hall and cited this case:
When Duke Liú Yǔduān went to Yúnjū Monastery to give thanks for rain,
he asked Hóngjué,
"Where does the rain come from?"
Hóngjué said,
"It comes from where Duke's question arises."
The Duke then made three bows joyfully and withdrew.
After walking several steps,
Hóngjué called out,
"Duke!"
The Duke turned his head.
Hóngjué said,
"Where does the question come from?"
The Duke was speechless.
Returning home, he died after three days.
The Master said:
"When Duke Liú Yǔduān was speechless and returned home,
dying after three days,
he was exactly scratching Hóngjué's itch.
Only he didn't know the way of turning about.
If at that moment, when told 'Where does the question come from,'
he had just as before made three bows joyfully and withdrawn, he would have made Hóngjué doubt for thirty years."
He ascended the hall.
Lifting his staff, he showed it to the assembly and said,
"Do you see?"
Then he thumped it once and said,
"Do you hear?"
If you say you truly see and truly hear,
you are precisely one who chases after sounds and forms.
Again raising it, he said,
"Do you see?"
Then he thumped it once more and said,
"Do you hear?"
If you say you do not see and do not hear,
you are precisely one who avoids forms and escapes sounds.
After all, how should it be?
Throwing it down, he said,
"The crane has nine marshes, yet its wings are hard to soar;
The horse lacks a thousand miles, vainly it chases the wind."
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
Whenever monks came to visit Lǔzǔ,
he would sit facing the wall.
One day, Nánquán arrived,
and also sat facing the wall.
Nánquán then patted him on the back with one palm.
Lǔzǔ asked, "Who?"
Nánquán said,
"Pǔyuàn."
Lǔzǔ said,
"What are you doing?"
Nánquán said,
"Just ordinary."
The Master said:
"Lowering the hook across the four seas, only to catch fierce dragons.
Transcendent mysteries seek a true confidant.
Though Elder Nánquán was adept at discerning capacities,
he should have recognized fortune and misfortune.
Yet he still failed to know where Lǔzǔ stood.
Now, is there anyone who knows where he stood?
Be careful not to speculate within the ghost cave."
Jiāng Lìngrén requests the ascension to the seat.
Birth is the birth of death.
Death is the death of birth.
Both paths are level and clear.
Without that and without this.
Since there is no birth or death, and no that or this.
Clearly, at the tips of the hundred grasses.
Clearly, the intention of the ancestral teacher.
Like the sky universally covering, like the earth universally supporting.
With one thought in accord, all is pure at once.
Addressing the assembly, he says:
Since there is no birth or death,
then as for the donor official,
what was it fifty-seven years ago?
And what is it fifty-seven years later?
After a long pause, he says:
Assembly, all raise your eyes high.
See how many strands my eyebrows have.
The Master ascended the hall and raised [a case].
A monk asked Mùzhōu:
"I won't ask about removing one layer with another layer.
But when not removing one layer with another layer, how is it?"
Mùzhōu said:
"Yesterday I planted eggplants.
Today I sow winter melons."
The Master said:
"Viewed from high above, they are insufficient;
Leveled from down below, they are more than enough.
Tomorrow in the hall, everyone can bite the eggplants horizontally or vertically as they please.
Is there anyone who can utter a single phrase about the winter melons?
If you can utter a single phrase,
Whether monastic or lay, sentient or insentient,
All will be fully satisfied, snoring contentedly.
If you cannot utter one,
Then return my meal money to me."
Ascending the hall.
The Dharma is the eternal Dharma.
The Way is the eternal Way.
Pressing until the face gate breaks.
Pointing, yet not reaching.
Shouting once.
The Master ascended the hall and cited [a case].
A monk asked Mùzhōu,
"What are words that unfold and expound?"
Mùzhōu said,
"Assign positions according to ability."
"What are words that do not unfold and expound?"
Mùzhōu said,
"We reverently offer this sacrifice."
The Master said,
"Mùzhōu, the ancient Buddha, skillfully responded to the incoming capacity.
Although this is so,
he only attained eighty percent.
If someone were to ask Jìngshān,
'What are words that unfold and expound?'
I would immediately tell him,
'Answering a hundred questions for every ten asked—what difficulty is there in that?'
'What are words that do not unfold and expound?'
[I would] shout once and say, 'Don't let the latrine boil over!'"
Vice Minister Wèi requests the ascension to the seat.
Residing in Chángshān County, Qúzhōu.
Wèi Gāng, observing mourning,
respectfully offers pure wealth to enter the mountain and perform the ceremony.
Still commanding this mountain dweller
to ascend this seat,
to proclaim and elucidate prajñā (wisdom).
With this merit,
to support and recommend his late father, the retired instructor of governance,
for rebirth in the Land of Peace and Nourishment (Sukhāvatī).
Do all of you know?
This elder lay devotee
is none other than Lord Wèi, who hosted three generations in Hézhōu.
When this mountain monk Dàguān first began wandering in the Dàguān era,
I also once visited his home.
The Vice Minister was still young then.
Today, serving as an official, he exerts effort for the state,
all due to the hidden virtue of his father.
This elder cultivated learning extensively throughout his life,
delighting in reading Buddhist texts,
associating with elder monks beyond worldly affairs,
and diligently practicing the pure conduct.
He often used Wáng Fànzhì's
"Earthen Bun" verses as Buddhist practice,
to awaken and enlighten the worldly.
Recently seeing the biographical account by Pan Shèrén,
which details his actual deeds.
Hearing that his illness had become critical,
when visitors came to inquire,
he still taught with compassion and guidance,
not uttering a single word about worldly matters.
At the moment of passing,
he was calm and composed, speaking and smiling as usual,
and passed away seated in the lotus posture.
As Vimalakīrti said: "If the body suffers,
remember the beings in the evil realms and give rise to great compassion.
Since I am already subdued,
I should also subdue all beings.
Only eliminate their afflictions, not the Dharma."
Then addressing the assembly, he said:
Lord Wèi's illness was critical,
yet he could endure suffering,
and expediently preach the Dharma for all who came,
sufficiently demonstrating the verification of his Buddhist practice.
Today, fortunate to encounter all of you in this gathering to bear witness together,
I cannot help but borrow his nostrils to breathe. Do you wish to know the Dharma?
It is Suchness, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, Nirvāṇa.
Do you wish to know the affliction?
It is deluded thoughts, inversions, greed, anger, and wrong views.
Even so,
apart from deluded thoughts and inversions,
there is no Suchness or Buddha-nature.
Apart from greed, anger, and wrong views,
there is no Bodhi or Nirvāṇa.
Now, tell me, is it separate or not separate?
If separate, preserving one and discarding the other deepens the affliction.
If not separate, it is precisely a muddled Buddha-nature and a vague Suchness.
After all, how can one explain the principle of eliminating the affliction without eliminating the Dharma?
Some fellows, hearing this, then say:
"The Dharma itself is the affliction,
the affliction itself is the Dharma.
All verbal expressions
lack true meaning.
Following Suchness, then inversions, deluded thoughts, greed, anger, and wrong views are all Dharma.
Following inversions, then Suchness, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, Nirvāṇa are all afflictions."
Such views—
do not say that I wear the monastic robe;
even being his lecture-master's slave
is not enough.
Why? One must know that on level ground, countless are the dead;
only those who clearly pass through the thorny forest are true adepts.
Have you not seen the ancients say:
"If there were a Dharma surpassing Nirvāṇa,
I would say it is like an illusion, like a dream."
If one can, within the dreamlike illusion,
truly realize, truly understand,
truly cultivate, truly practice,
with the true Dharma,
able to subdue oneself,
give rise to great compassion,
and employ various skillful means,
further able to subdue all beings,
yet regarding beings, not having the notion of subduing or not subduing,
also not having the notion of inversion,
not having the notion of greed, anger, or wrong views,
not having the notion of Suchness, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, or Nirvāṇa,
not having the notion of eliminating affliction,
not eliminating the Dharma,
not having the notion of preserving one, discarding one, separate or not separate.
Since there are no such notions,
then one path is pure, equal, and liberated.
Jìngshān today speaks this Dharma of purity, equality, and liberation,
dedicated to Wèi Gāng in mourning,
to transfer merit for his late father, the retired instructor of governance.
I humbly pray
that he may realize the Pure Land of mind-only,
behold the Amitābha of self-nature,
and find joy in this realm and others, wherever he may be.
Again addressing the assembly, he said:
Now that I have borrowed his nostrils to breathe,
today Jìngshān will instead use his own nostrils to breathe for him.
He gives a shout.
Ascending the hall to mark the end of the summer retreat.
The case that began on the fifteenth day of the fourth month,
is only concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Now, among the many gathered here,
each has their own reasoning, difficult to clarify.
Is there anyone in the assembly with sharp eloquence and quick words?
Step forward and try to clarify it.
Even if you manage to clarify it,
you must still press your forehead to the ground before it's acceptable.
The master ascended the hall and cited
Yúnmén's saying:
"One must reach the state where nothing obstructs the eye,
penetrate the nature of names and phrases.
All dharmas are empty—mountains, rivers, and the great earth are but names.
Even these names cannot be grasped.
This is called the samādhi ocean where all natures are complete,
yet it remains like waves rippling without wind.
One must ultimately transcend knowing in awakening—
for awakening itself is Buddha-nature.
This is called the person of no affairs."
But you must further know there exists the pivotal aperture beyond.
The master said:
"Pouring oil to extinguish fire is trivial matter;
adding frost to snow truly vexes mortals."
Ascending the hall.
Tearing down the eastern fence to mend the western wall.
At Jìngshān's gate, there is no fixed standard.
If there were a standard, who would understand it thoroughly?
The monks' hall sees through the kitchen of fragrant accumulation.
The owl's beak bites to death the ridge of the Buddha hall.
Entering the hall.
A monk asked:
"Cuīwēi made offerings to the arhats,
while Dānxiá burned the wooden Buddha.
I wonder about these two venerable masters -
which one was right?"
The master said:
"Which one was wrong?"
The monk continued:
"Then who gets the middle way?"
The master said:
"Just keep groping around."
The monk continued:
"Why do they all appear horizontally and vertically on the staff's head?"
The master said:
"What are your blurred eyes doing?"
The monk continued:
"Is this the way you help people?"
The master said: "Yes."
Then he said:
"Dānxiá burning the wooden Buddha
defies human sentiment.
Cuīwēi making offerings to arhats
follows conventional precepts.
But at Jìngshān's gate,
both are useless.
So what does Jìngshān's gate use?
When autumn rivers run clear and shallow,
White dew blends with misty isles.
How wonderful is Guānshìyīn,
Whose entire body enters the wild grass."
Ascending the hall.
Before this mountain monk left his hometown,
more than eighty days ago, I had already explained it clearly for everyone.
Today's matter is finished.
How about today's matter? Shout!
One shout.
Ascending the hall.
A monk asked,
"Where a thousand sages cannot reach,
The ten thousand dharmas function without deficiency.
What is Jìngshān's pivotal device?"
The master said,
"A coiled true dragon would rather hide in troubled waters."
The monk continued,
"Vast and expansive, the dharma realm is fully revealed;
Clear and distinct, the ancestral mechanism shines alone."
The master said,
"Heaven rotates left, earth turns right."
The monk continued,
"The whole substance comes thus,
The whole substance goes thus."
The master said,
"You've exhausted yourself, elder." Then he said,
"The true mind dwells nowhere, true illumination exists alone.
The true nature transcends all conditioning.
True seeing does not depend on objects.
True wisdom is unobstructed, true insight is boundless.
Above, it merges with the source of all buddhas;
Below, it accords with the mind-ground of all beings.
Therefore it is said,
Everywhere true, everywhere true,
Every speck of dust is the original person.
When speaking of reality, sound does not appear;
The majestic true body loses itself."
Then, looking at the assembly, he said,
"What is the majestic true body?"
"Gazing at the water's edge from the cliff,
One deliberately invites a wave of sorrow."
Ascending the hall.
Where wisdom does not reach, be cautious not to speak.
If you speak, horns will sprout.
Raising the whisk, he said:
Even with horns grown, is it a donkey or a horse?
Do you recognize it?
If you recognize it,
you may well walk among different beings.
If you fail to recognize it,
you will sink into eternal transmigration.
The Master ascended the hall and cited:
A monk asked Tóuzǐ,
"How is it when the moon is not yet full?"
Tóuzǐ said,
"Swallow three or four."
The monk said,
"How about after it becomes full?"
Tóuzǐ said,
"Spit out seven or eight."
The Master said,
"Three and four,
seven and eight—
the numbers are quite clear,
yet no one can count them."
Since the numbers are clearly defined,
why can no one count them?
After a long pause, he said:
"A Daoist wearing a white robe
is not truly a scholar."
The master ascended the hall.
A monk bowed, rose, and immediately gave a shout.
The master also gave a shout.
The monk returned to the assembly.
The master said,
"Still lacking one move."
Then he said,
"One shout distinguishes guest and host;
illumination and function are simultaneously enacted.
If you wish to understand the meaning within,
it is like striking the third watch at noon.
Now tell me, just now this monk's shout
and this mountain monk's shout—
which is guest and which is host?
Which is illumination and which is function?
If you can discern this,
you are permitted to walk alone throughout the great chiliocosm.
But if not,
be careful not to lose your spoon and chopsticks in the alms bowl."
He then gave another shout.
On New Year's Day, the Dharma drum was newly mounted as I ascended the hall.
The new year strikes the new drum.
Universally bestowing the new Dharma rain.
All things follow renewal.
Each and every one conforms to the rules.
The great being Samantabhadra rejoices.
Seizing the moment to open the gate.
Releasing the white elephant king.
Nowhere to be found across the land.
Lifting his staff, he said:
Only this is not subject to old or new.
Casually opening its mouth, it swallows the Dharma body.
Throwing it down, he said:
What is this?
Within a thousand-year-old peach pit,
Originally lies the same old kernel.
The Master ascended the hall and brought up [a case]:
A monk asked Zhàozhōu,
"I, a student, have newly entered the monastic community.
I beg the Master for instruction."
Zhàozhōu said,
"Have you finished eating your gruel or not?"
The monk said,
"I have finished eating the gruel."
Zhàozhōu said,
"Then go wash your bowl."
The monk suddenly experienced great enlightenment.
The Master [Yúnmén] said,
"Is it truly so or not?"
Yúnmén said,
"Just tell me, was there instruction or was there no instruction?
If you say there was,
then what did he tell him?
If you say there was not,
then why did this monk become enlightened?"
The Master further said,
"Zhàozhōu and this monk,
if it were not for Yúnmén,
would have been wronged their whole lives.
Nowadays, there is a kind of blind fellow in various places,
who often completely interprets this as just a story about washing the bowl."
Ascending the hall.
This morning is the fifteenth of the first month.
There is an old case.
Light several bowls of lamps.
Beat the drum and invite all to look.
Looking is not without merit.
But when suddenly the oil runs out and the lamps extinguish,
In the darkness, beware of bumping into the pillar.
Ascending the hall.
The mind of the great immortal from India.
Secretly transmitted east and west.
What is the mind that is transmitted?
Shouting once, striking the meditation seat once, saying:
What words are these?
Zhuàngyuán Zhāng and Zhuàngyuán Wáng arrived at the main hall.
A monk asked Yúnmén:
"What is the master's family tradition?"
Yúnmén said:
"When scholars come to visit."
The master said:
"The scholar is already here.
How should we meet with him?"
Then looking left and right he said:
"None but foes will the world bring together."
The master ascended the hall and cited [the case]:
A monk asked Tóuzǐ, "What is the Ten-Body Tamer?"
Tóuzǐ got down from his rope-bed and stood.
[The monk] asked again,
"How much difference is there between the ordinary and the sage?"
Tóuzǐ also got down from his rope-bed and stood.
The master said:
"Tóuzǐ gets down from his rope-bed—
today I bring it up for elucidation.
You fellows before the donkey and behind the horse,
be careful not to misinterpret it."
The master ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"Does a person of great spiritual practice still fall within cause and effect?"
Former Bǎizhàng said,
"Does not fall within cause and effect."
Why then did he fall into the body of a wild fox?
The master said,
"When meeting people, just bring this up."
The monk continued,
Just as later Bǎizhàng said 'does not obscure cause and effect,'
why did he escape the wild fox body?
The master said,
"When meeting people, just bring this up."
The monk continued,
"If someone were to ask Jìngshān,
'Does a person of great spiritual practice still fall within cause and effect?'
I wonder what the master would say to him?"
The master said,
"Say to him,
'When meeting people, just bring this up.'"
Then he said,
"A person of great spiritual practice falls within cause and effect."
Striking the meditation seat once with his whisk, he said:
"Still not apart from this message."
"A person of great spiritual practice does not fall within cause and effect."
Again striking the meditation seat once, he said:
"Still not apart from this message."
Whether falling or not falling - with one stroke of the brush,
then what can be called cause and effect?
Again striking the meditation seat once, he said:
"Still not apart from this message."
Then raising his whisk, he addressed the assembly:
"The message from five hundred lifetimes ago is present here -
No need to search elsewhere in your minds."
The Master ascended the platform.
The Patriarch said:
"If the eye does not sleep, all dreams naturally cease.
If the mind does not discriminate, all dharmas are of one suchness.
What is the eye that does not sleep?
What is the mind that does not discriminate?
Mountain blossoms bloom like brocade.
Stream waters lie deep as indigo."
Ascending the hall.
The root of sentient beings relies on the ocean of wisdom as its source.
The flow of conscious beings takes the Dharma body as their essence.
So, what is the source of the ocean of wisdom?
What is the essence of the Dharma body?
If one recognizes this source,
a thousand sources, ten thousand sources are just one source.
If one recognizes this essence,
a thousand essences, ten thousand essences are just one essence.
Therefore, it is said:
In the boundless realms of the universe,
self and others are not separated by even a hair's breadth.
Across the ten ages of past and present,
