They certainly don't like those who speak of mind and nature.
They only like sharp, swift exchanges,

Those who like to speak of mind and nature

They only like the intricate weaving of threads,

this is precisely useless,

turning smoothly like a wheel,

Under the Sixth Patriarch, the sayings of National Teacher Zhōng are the most numerous,

In the forests, it's called the story of the National Teacher calling the attendant three times.

A monk asked:
"What is the mind of the ancient buddhas?"
The National Teacher said:
"Walls, tiles, and pebbles are."
The Master said:
Answering like this,
if the subtle path of understanding,
the mind not severed, the life-root not cut,
the great Dharma not clarified,
one certainly wouldn't dare be like this.
The four edges collapse to the ground; a shout, a strike, a push, a press—
the spark from struck stone, the lightning flash—these are easy.
This kind of speaking is hard to handle.
As mentioned before, his house is vast, his gate great,
the Dharma-nature broad, the waves wide.
Only when the life-root is cut can one be thus.
The monk said:
"Walls, tiles, and pebbles—aren't they insentient?"
The National Teacher said:
"Yes."
The monk said: "Can the insentient still expound the Dharma?"
The National Teacher said:
"Constantly expounding, blazingly expounding, without interruption."
The monk said:
"Why don't I hear it?"
The National Teacher said:
"You yourself do not hear.
You cannot hinder those who do hear."
The monk said:
"I am uncertain, what kind of person can hear?"
The National Teacher said:
"The sages can hear."
The monk asked:
"Does the Venerable still hear?"
National Teacher said:
"I do not hear."
The monk said:
"Since the Venerable doesn't hear,"
"how do you know insentient beings expound the Dharma?"
National Teacher said:
"Fortunately, I don't hear."
"If I heard,"
"I would be equal to the saints."
"Then you wouldn't hear me expound the Dharma."
The monk said:
"If so, then ordinary beings have no share."
National Teacher said:
"I speak for ordinary beings,"
"not for the saints."
The monk said:
"After ordinary beings hear, what happens?"
National Teacher said:
"Then they are no longer ordinary beings."
The Master said:
"Marvelous! Look at him -"
"rolling along without sticking in one corner,"
"not failing the questioner."
"'Fortunately, I don't hear.'"
"'If I heard, I would be equal to the saints.'"
"'Then you wouldn't hear me expound the Dharma.'"
"Can you call this sloppy?"
"Without obtaining the heart-marrow of all buddhas and ancestors,"
"how could he turn like this?"
"Don't say there's no gain or loss."
"This is having gain and loss within no gain and loss,"
"and no gain and loss within having gain and loss."
"This is called entering mud, entering water,"
"riding a thief's horse to chase the thief gang,"
"borrowing a granny's skirt to bow to the granny."
"How difficult to handle!"
Another monk asked:
"Having resolved to leave home intending to seek buddhahood,"
"I'm unsure how to use the mind to attain buddhahood."
National Teacher said:
"When no mind can be used, then you attain buddhahood."
The Master said:
"This monk was hard to handle."
"Just like a burdock seed."
"This old man was soft and stubborn,"
"and met this soft stubborn monk who stuck to him."
He then asked:
"If no mind can be used, who attains buddhahood?"
National Teacher said:
"No mind itself attains buddhahood."
"Attaining buddhahood also has no mind."
The monk said:
"The Buddha has great inconceivability,"
"being able to save sentient beings."
"If there's no mind,"
"who saves sentient beings?"
National Teacher said:
"No mind truly saves beings."
"If you see beings that can be saved,"
"that is having mind."
"Clearly this is birth and death."
The monk said:
"Now since there's no mind,"
"why did the Able One appear in the world and speak so many teachings?"
"Could these be empty words?"
National Teacher said:
"The Buddha's teaching also has no mind."
The monk said:
"If teaching Dharma has no mind,"
"shouldn't there be no teaching?"
National Teacher said:
"Teaching is none, none is teaching." The monk said:
"If teaching Dharma has no mind, does creating karma have mind?"
National Teacher said:
"No mind means no karma."
"Now since there is karma,"
"mind is birth and death."
"How can there be no mind?"
The monk said:
"No mind then attains buddhahood."
"Has the Venerable attained buddhahood now?"
National Teacher said:
"Mind itself doesn't exist,"
"who speaks of attaining buddhahood?"
"If there's buddhahood to attain,"
"that still has mind."
"Having mind means having outflows."
"Where can no mind be found?"
The monk said:
"Since there's no buddhahood to attain,"
"does the Venerable still have buddha-function?"
National Teacher said:
"Mind itself doesn't exist,"
"how could function come from?"
The monk said:
"Vast emptiness with nothing - doesn't this fall into nihilism?"
National Teacher said:
"Originally there's no view,"
"who speaks of nihilism?"
The monk said:
"Originally there's no view,"
"doesn't this fall into emptiness?"
National Teacher said:
"There's no emptiness to fall into."
The monk said:
"Is there something to fall into?"
National Teacher said:
"Since emptiness is nothing,"
"how could falling be established?"
The monk said:
"When both subject and object are absent,"
"if someone comes with a knife to take your life,"
"is this existence or nonexistence?"
National Teacher said:
"It is nonexistence."
The monk said:
"Is there pain?"
National Teacher said:
"Pain is also nonexistent."
The monk said:
"Since there's no pain,"
"after death what path is born into?"
National Teacher said:
"No death, no birth, also no path."
The monk said:
"Since attaining effortless freedom,"
"when pressed by hunger and cold, how to use the mind?"
National Teacher said:
"Hungry then eat, cold then wear clothes."
The monk said:
"Knowing hunger and cold,"
"must involve having mind."
National Teacher said:
"I ask you about having mind -"
"what form does mind take?"
The monk hesitated for a long time seeking mind's form regarding hunger and cold,
but couldn't find it at all.
Finally he reported truthfully:
"Mind has no form."
National Teacher said:
"Since you know it has no form,"
"this is originally no mind."
"How can you say there is?"
The monk said:
"When meeting tigers and wolves in the mountains,"
"how to use the mind?"
National Teacher said:
"See as if not seeing,"
"come as if not coming."
"If they have no mind,"
"savage beasts cannot harm you."
The monk said:
"Tranquil without affairs,"
"solitary and free with no mind -"
"what is this called?"
National Teacher said:
"Called Vajra Great Being."
The Master shouted and said:
"Good person unwilling to be, yet wants to lie in shit!"
The monk said:
"What form does Vajra Great Being have?"
National Teacher said:
"Originally without form."
The Master said:
"Why not say so earlier?"
The monk said:
"Since there's no form,"
"what thing is called Vajra Great Being?"
National Teacher said:
"Called formless Vajra Great Being."
The monk said:
"What merit does Vajra Great Being have?"
National Teacher said:
"One thought corresponding with vajra,"
"can extinguish kalpas of生死 heavy sins numerous as Ganges sands,"
"enabling one to see buddhas numerous as Ganges sands."
"The Vajra Great Being's merit is immeasurable,"
"not spoken by mouth,"
"not conceived by thought."
"Even if explaining for kalpas numerous as Ganges sands,"

This monk immediately had great awakening,
like waking from sleep,
like a lotus blooming.
Such ones are vajra circles and chestnut burrs -
if you can't swallow them or penetrate them,

you'll certainly slander without doubt.
Penetrating here,
one can become a great boat,
not attached to this shore,
not attached to that shore,
not dwelling in midstream.
Good friends who can employ such methods and enter such dens

Without possessing such discriminating eyes,

preferring such talk instead.
But they mistakenly take it as substantial dharma.
Those who gain entry through single opportunity, single situation, single shout, single strike
certainly dislike such talk.
This is also mistaken understanding.
Truly what's seen differs, each having gains and losses.
As scriptures say: Bodhisattvas see water as nectar,
devas see water as crystal,
ordinary people see water as water,
hungry ghosts see water as pus and blood.
Perhaps some monk loving lofty Chan
comes out saying:

Then tell him:

Therefore it's included in the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
A monk asked National Teacher Huìzhōng:
"An ancient virtue said:"
"'Lush green bamboos are entirely Dharma body,'"
"'luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than prajñā.'"
"Some disapprove, calling it heterodox,"
"others believe, calling it inconceivable. I don't know which is correct."
National Teacher said:
"This is the realm of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī,"
"not what ordinary petty people can believe and accept."
"All accord with the meaning of Mahāyāna definitive sutras."
"Thus the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:"
"The Buddha's body fills the dharma realm,"
"manifesting universally before all beings."
"Responding to conditions, meeting feelings, nowhere not reaching,"
"yet constantly abiding on this bodhi seat."
"Since green bamboos don't leave the dharma realm,"
"how could they not be Dharma body?"
"Also the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:"
"Form is boundless, therefore prajñā is boundless."
"Since yellow flowers don't transcend form,"
"how could they not be prajñā?"
"Profound and distant words,"
"those who don't understand find hard to comprehend."
Also, a Huáyán lecturer asked Great Pearl Monk:
"Why does the Chan Master disapprove of 'lush green bamboos are entirely Dharma body, luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than prajñā'?"
Great Pearl said:
"Dharma body has no form,"
"responding to green bamboos it manifests shape."
"Prajñā has no knowing,"
"facing yellow flowers it reveals appearance."
"Not that those yellow flowers and green bamboos possess prajñā and Dharma body."
"Thus the sutra says:"
"The Buddha's true Dharma body is like space,"
"responding to things manifesting forms like moon in water."
"If yellow flowers were prajñā,"
"prajñā would equal insentience."
"If green bamboos were Dharma body,"
"could green bamboos still function?"
"Lecturer, do you understand?"
The lecturer said:
"I don't understand this meaning."
Great Pearl said:
"For those who see nature,"
"saying 'it is' is fine,"
"saying 'it isn't' is fine - speaking according to function,"
"not stuck in right and wrong."
"For those who don't see nature,"
"speaking of green bamboos they cling to green bamboos,"
"speaking of yellow flowers they cling to yellow flowers,"
"speaking of Dharma body they stagnate in Dharma body,"
"speaking of prajñā they don't recognize prajñā."
"Therefore all become arguments."
The Master said:
"National Teacher advocated 'lush green bamboos are entirely Dharma body',"
"advocating straight to the end."
"Great Pearl refuted 'green bamboos are not Dharma body',"
"refuting straight to the end."
"This old man takes the advocate"
"and the refuter,"
"gathers them together without further comment,"
"not daring to move them one slightest bit."
"I want you learners to have the eye"
"to penetrate National Teacher's vajra circle,"
"and swallow Great Pearl's chestnut burr."
"Those with the eye can distinguish,"
"those without will likely laugh."
"Although Zōnggǎo studied under Master Yuánwù and lost his nose,"
"originally the one who gave me a nose"
"was Master Zhàntáng - only when teaching others his blade wasn't sharp enough."
"If discussing Chan sicknesses, no one surpasses him."
"I once considered a story from the scriptures:"
"Yaṅgīlamāla wanted a thousand finger-bones to make a flower crown before ascending the throne, already having 999 fingers,"
"lacking only one finger."
"He wanted to cut his mother's finger to complete the count."
"The Buddha knew his conditions were ripe,"
"so went to convert him."
"Just as Yaṅgīla intended"
"to cut his mother's finger,"
"suddenly hearing the ringing of a monk's staff,"
"he abandoned his mother's finger"
"and asked the Buddha for one finger, saying:"
"Since Gautama is here,"
"I beg you to give me one finger to fulfill my wish."
"Just as he raised the knife,"
"the World-Honored One pulled away and left."
"The World-Honored One walked slowly,"
"Yaṅgīla hurried but couldn't catch up."
Then he shouted loudly:
"Stop, stop!"
The World-Honored One said:
"I stopped long ago."
"It's you who hasn't stopped."
Yaṅgīla suddenly awakened,
and joined the Buddha to leave home.
The Buddha then had him take a bowl to a elder's door.
"The household woman was experiencing difficult childbirth."
The elder said:
"Gautama's disciple,"
"you being supremely sage,"
"what method can relieve childbirth difficulty?"
Yaṅgīla said:
"I've newly entered the Way,"
"not knowing this method."
"Wait while I return to ask the World-Honored One,"
"then come back to report."
Returning, he reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Yaṅgīla:
"Go quickly and tell her:"
"'Since following the sage's Dharma,'"
"'I've never killed living beings.'"
Yaṅgīla immediately followed the Buddha's words,
went and told her.
The woman heard this and was relieved from childbirth difficulty.
The Master said:
"Here, using sticks or shouts,"
"overturning the meditation seat,"
"quoting scriptures to discuss principles and phenomena,"
"stone-spark lightning-flash -"
"can you catch the black chicken at midnight?"
When I asked Master Zhàntáng for instruction,
just as I brought up this story,
Zhàntáng said:
"You've scratched my itch."
"This story is a gold-shit dharma -"
"not understanding, it's like gold;"
"understanding, it's like shit."
I said: "Is there no skillful means?"
Zhàntáng said:
"I have skillful means,"
"but you simply don't understand."
I said: "I beg the Venerable's compassion."
Zhàntáng said:
"Yaṅgīla said:"
"'I've newly entered the Way, not knowing this method.'"
Waiting to ask the World-Honored One.
Before reaching the Buddha's seat,
how was it when a household gave birth to a son?
Since I came through the sage's dharma,
I have never killed any living being.
Yāngjué, holding these words, had not yet reached the household
when the son had already been born—how was it then?
This old man couldn't comprehend it at the time.
Later, while at Hǔqiū,
reading the Huáyán Sūtra,
I reached the passage where the bodhisattva ascends to the seventh stage and realizes the patience of the unproduced dharmas, which says:
O son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes this patience,
immediately he enters the bodhisattva's eighth immovable stage,
becoming a profoundly practicing bodhisattva,
difficult to know, without distinctions,
free from all appearances, all thoughts, all attachments.
Countless, boundless śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas
cannot reach it.
Apart from all disputes,
tranquil extinction manifests before him.
It is like a bhikṣu possessing spiritual powers,
attaining mastery of mind,
progressing sequentially until entering the cessation samādhi:
all stirrings of mind, recollections, thoughts, and discriminations
completely cease. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise.
Abiding in the immovable stage,
he immediately abandons all effort-based practices,
attaining the effortless dharma of body, speech, and mind activities.
All tasks of thought cease,
dwelling in spontaneous action.
It is like a person dreaming of falling into a great river,
and to cross it, he exerts great courage and applies great expedients.
Through exerting great courage and applying expedients,
he suddenly awakens.
Having awakened, all his efforts cease.
So too is the bodhisattva.
Seeing sentient beings immersed in the four streams,
to save them, he exerts great courage and arouses great vigor.
Through this courage and vigor, he reaches this immovable stage.
Having reached it, all efforts completely cease;
the characteristics and activities of dual practices no longer appear.
In this bodhisattva mahāsattva,
the bodhisattva-mind, the buddha-mind,
the mind of bodhi, the mind of nirvāṇa
do not even arise,
how much less the mind of the world.
The master said:
Reaching here, the carrying-pole is lost.
The expedient means Zhàntáng explained to me
suddenly appeared before me.
Only then did I know that a true good friend does not deceive me.
Truly it is a vajra circle,
which can only be penetrated when the ālaya-vijñāna is clear.
There was another venerable
called Monk Luòpǔ,
who long served as Línjì's attendant.
Jì often praised him,
calling him an arrow under Línjì's gate—
precisely to challenge people.
After traveling, he went straight to Jiāshān's peak, where he built a hut and stayed for a year.
Jiāshān, knowing this, wrote a letter and sent a monk swiftly to deliver it.
Luòpǔ received it and immediately sat down,
then extended his hand again, demanding [the letter].
The monk had no reply.
Pǔ then struck him, saying:
Go back and report to the venerable.
The monk returned and reported to Jiāshān.
Shān said:
This monk, if he reads the letter, will come within three days.
If he does not read the letter,
this person cannot be saved.
The master said:
The ancients called this fishing for people.
Who knows what idle words are in the letter?
Yet Luòpǔ swallowed his hook and line;
within three days, he indeed came.
Jiāshān预先 had someone watch for him to leave his hut,
then burned his dwelling.
The master said:
This alone is a vajra circle.
Pǔ paid no heed.
The master said:
To become a buddha or patriarch, one must be such a person.
He went straight to Jiāshān's abbot's quarters,
did not bow, but stood facing him with hands folded.
Shān said:
A chicken roosting in a phoenix nest is not of the same kind—get out!
Pǔ said:
From afar I've rushed to your breeze,
begging the master to receive me.
Shān said:
Before me there is no ācārya,
here there is no old monk.
Pǔ then shouted.
Shān said:
Hold, hold! Don't be hasty and careless.
Clouds and moon are the same, streams and mountains differ; cutting off all people's tongues is not impossible,
but how can you, ācārya, make a tongueless person understand speech?
The master said:

one must awaken by oneself to attain it.
Attaining it in the mind, responding with the hand.
If you haven't reached a place of peace and joy,
constantly seeking knowledge and views, looking for understanding,
such poisoned thoughts entering the mind
are like oil entering flour -
never to be extracted.
Even if extracted,
it still requires much dealing with.
This matter is like the blue sky and bright sun -
originally without obstructions,
yet obscured by these poisoned thoughts.
Therefore, one cannot attain freedom in the dharma.
This old man always appreciated Zhēnjìng和尚 saying:
"Nowadays most people attain a state where body and mind are extinguished,
the before and after cut off,
ceasing and resting, one thought for ten thousand years,
like an incense burner in an old temple,
cold and desolate,
and consider this the ultimate.
They don't realize
they are obscured by these sublime states,
their own correct knowledge cannot manifest,
their spiritual powers and light cannot shine forth.
Or else they cling to 'the ordinary mind is the Way,'
considering it the ultimate.
Heaven is heaven, earth is earth,
mountains are mountains, waters are waters,
monks are monks, laypeople are laypeople,
full months have thirty days,
short months twenty-nine.
In all activities,
they must follow the ordinary path, considering it secure.
Fixedly holding to it, conforming to it,
not daring to take another step,
afraid of falling into pits and chasms.
Long like two blind people walking,
a walking stick that cannot be abandoned for an inch,
tightly grasping it, relying on it,
step by step dependent.
One day, when the dharma-eye clears,
suddenly realizing previous errors,
throwing away the stick,
releasing both hands,
the ten directions vast and open,
seven verticals and eight horizontals,
east, west, south, north -
nothing not permissible.
Only here does one attain freedom.
How many people today can let go of the stick and release their hands?
Formerly, when Zhēnjìng和尚's new record was published,
my old teacher was in Wǔzǔ's hall,
serving as head monk.
One day Wǔzǔ saw a monk in the corridor
holding a volume of writing.
Zǔ asked:
"What writing is in your hand?"
The monk said:
"It's Zhēnjìng和尚's record."
Zǔ then took it and read it,
immediately praising:
"How admirable that in this degenerate age there is such a venerable!"
Then he called for the head monk.
My old teacher was at that time washing in the back room.
Hearing the call, he hurried out.
Zǔ said:
"I've obtained a volume of writing -
truly inconceivable!
What's called skillfully expressing the essential dharma.
You try reading it:
'Ceasing and resting,
one thought for ten thousand years,
the before and after cut off.'
How many in various places today have reached this state?
Yet he calls it sublime states.
Formerly at Bǎofēng there was a Guǎng道人,
exactly this kind of person - his whole body unattended to,
not seeing worldly affairs at all,
worldly dust unable to stain him.
Even so,
he was obscured by these sublime states, blocking his dharma-eye.
You should know: reaching where not a single thought arises, before and after cut off,
truly requires a venerable,
like Shuǐlǎo和尚.
While gathering vines,
he asked Mǎzǔ:
"What is the meaning of the patriarch coming from the west?"
Zǔ said:
"Come closer and I'll tell you."
As Shuǐlǎo approached, Mǎzǔ kicked him in the chest, knocking him down.
Shuǐlǎo suddenly experienced great awakening,
unconsciously got up laughing heartily.
Zǔ said:
"What principle have you seen?"
Lǎo said:
"Hundreds of thousands of dharma gates, immeasurable subtle meanings -
on a single hair's tip
I recognize the source."
In this teaching,
this is called 'entering the stream, forgetting the object.'
When what is entered becomes quiet,
the two characteristics of movement and stillness
clearly do not arise.
Just attaining an entry point,
one forgets the characteristic of concentration.
When the characteristic of concentration is forgotten,
one doesn't fall into existence,
nor fall into non-existence.
The two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise -
this is Guānyīn's gate of entering principle.
Having awakened,
he opened his own treasury,
brought out his family treasure,
saying:
"Hundreds of thousands of dharma gates, immeasurable subtle meanings -
on a single hair's tip
I recognize the source."
Again laughing heartily.
Mǎzǔ, knowing he had reached this state, paid him no further attention,
nor gave any subsequent words.
Later dwelling at Shuǐlǎo hermitage,
when Chan practitioners came to visit,
he had a hundred or so followers.
When expounding, he would show off about this kick, saying:
"Since eating Mǎshī's kick,
Until now I haven't stopped laughing."

Did he ever speak of layered peaks emerald green, valley streams murmuring, river willows veiled in mist, courtyard flowers smiling in sunlight, orioles singing in tall trees, butterflies dancing among fragrant blossoms?
He only said:
"Since eating Mǎshī's kick,
Until now I haven't stopped laughing."
This is the first example of 'entering the stream, forgetting the object, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly not arising.'
Again, remember when Yúnmén asked Dòngshān:
"Where have you come from recently?"
Shān said:
"Chádù."
Mén said:
"Where did you spend summer?"
Shān said:
"Húnán Bàocí."
Mén said:
"When did you leave that mountain?"
He said: "The twenty-fifth of August."
Mén said:
"I spare you three beatings."
The ancients, simple and honest, answered truthfully,
thinking to himself:
"This time I truly came from Chádù.
What fault is there
to say
'spare me three beatings'?"
A true great man
must settle this with the old fellow.
The next day he went and asked:
"Yesterday the master spared me three beatings -
I don't know where the fault lies?"
He asked:
"Rice bag!
Jiāngxī, Húnán -
you just go like that?"
Dòngshān suddenly experienced great awakening.
There was no message to convey,
no principle to point out,
he only bowed in reverence.
Having awakened,
he opened his own treasury,
brought out his family treasure,
saying:
"Later I'll dwell in a grass hut where no people are,
not storing a single grain of rice,
not planting a single stalk of vegetable,
receiving all coming from the ten directions,
completely removing their nails and pulling out their wedges,
taking off their greasy hats,
removing their stinking hemp robes,
making them clean and refreshed as patch-robed monks.
Wouldn't that be splendid!"
Yúnmén said:
"Your body is only coconut-sized,
yet you open such a big mouth."
This is the second example of 'entering the stream, forgetting the object, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly not arising.'
Again, Gǔshān Yàn national teacher was at Xuěfēng's for many years.
One day Xuěfēng, knowing his conditions were ripe,
suddenly rose and grabbed him, saying:
"What is it?"
Yàn was liberated and awakened,
only raising his hand and waving.
Fēng said:
"Are you making principles?"
Yàn said:
"What principles are there?"
Later Yáng Dànián included this in the Transmission of the Lamp record,
calling it 'forgetting the understanding mind.'
This is the third example of 'entering the stream, forgetting the object, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly not arising.'
Again, Guànxī和尚,
one day seeing Línjì,
as Jì descended from his seat and grabbed him,
Xī immediately said:
"I understand, I understand."
This is the fourth example of 'entering the stream, forgetting the object, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly not arising.'
This cannot be explained to people,
cannot be transmitted to people.
This old man practiced for seventeen years -
I awakened fragmentarily here and there.
I understood some under Yúnmén's school,
under Cáodòng's school I also understood some,
only I couldn't attain the cutting off of before and after.
Later, in the capital at Tiānníng,
seeing my old teacher ascend the hall,
citing a monk asking Yúnmén:
"What is the place where all buddhas emerge?"
Mén said:
"East mountain walks on water."
If it were Tiānníng, he would not say thus:
"What is the place where all buddhas emerge?
The warm breeze comes from the south, the hall and pavilion grow slightly cool."
Here, suddenly before and after were cut off,
like a tangled skein of silk cut through with one stroke of a knife.
At that time, sweat poured from my whole body.
Although moving characteristics did not arise,
I was stuck in a bare and naked place.
One day going for interview,
my old teacher said:
"It's not easy for you to reach this state.
Pity you're dead and cannot come alive.
Not doubting words and phrases
is the great disease.
Haven't you heard:
Letting go at the cliff edge, willingly accepting responsibility;
Reviving after extinction, unable to deceive the ruler.
You must believe there is this principle."
This old man said to himself:
"According to my present attainment,
I'm already happy -
I can't understand any further."
My old teacher then had me stay in Zémù lodge as an unattached attendant.
Daily with scholars and officials,
I had to enter for interview three or four times.
He only raised 'having phrases, no phrases, like vines clinging to trees.'
As soon as I opened my mouth, he would say:
"Wrong!"
Thus for half a year
I just kept investigating.
One day, with various officials in the abbot's quarters during medicine meal,
I held chopsticks in hand,
completely forgetting to eat.
My old teacher said:
"This fellow investigates like boxwood Chan -
it shrinks back instead."
I then offered an analogy:
"Master,
this principle
is exactly like a dog looking at a pot of hot oil:
it wants to lick but cannot lick,
cannot,
wants to abandon but cannot abandon."
My old teacher said:
"Your analogy is excellent.
Just this is the diamond hoop and chestnut thorn bush."
One day, asking my old teacher,
"I've heard it said..."
The monk was at that time with the Fifth Patriarch.
He once brought up this topic.
I don't know how the Fifth Patriarch answered.
The monk was unwilling to say.
This old man said:
"At that time, you shouldn't have asked alone.
You should have asked before the assembly.
What harm is there in speaking of it now?"
The old monk then said:
"I asked:
'When there are words and no words, like a vine clinging to a tree, what then?'
The Patriarch said:
'It cannot be depicted,
nor can it be drawn.'
I asked again:
'What if suddenly the tree falls and the vine withers?'
The Patriarch said:
'It follows along.'"
As soon as this old man heard this account, he understood.
He then said:
"I have comprehended."
The old monk said:
"I only fear you haven't penetrated the gōng'àn."
This old man said:
"Please, Venerable, present one."
The old monk then proceeded to present a series of perplexing gōng'àns.
With two or three turns, I cut them off.
It was like finding a path in times of peace and proceeding without any obstruction.
The old monk said:
"Only now do I know
I haven't deceived you."
After I had understood,
I instead became doubtful about several Chán topics.
So I asked the old monk.
The old monk said:
"My Chán is like the great ocean.
If you can bring the great ocean,
then you may pour and take away.
But if you only bring a bowl,
and take away just a little before stopping,
then your capacity is only that much.
What can I do about it?
How many can reach your level?
In the past, there was only Elder Jǐng,
who was like you.
But he has passed away."
After some time had passed,
he brought up:
"After I established the monastic community, when I was later in the head monk's quarters at Yúnjū Monastery,
at night I often entered the chamber with fellow practitioners.
The old monk loved to come and listen.
Sometimes after the chamber session,
I would go up to the abbot's room.
I would see the old monk,
and we would sit together by the fireplace.
The old monk said:
'If there were a Chán practitioner
like this old monk,
how would you handle him?'
This old man said:
'What fortune that would be!
Just as Sū Dōngpō said, it's like an executioner getting a fat man to dismember.'
I then turned it around and entered the chamber with the old monk.
Pressed by me to the wall,
the old monk laughed heartily."
Reflecting on this old monk,
even if my bones were ground and body shattered, I could not repay him.
Because I paid respects to the elder, this old man recounts:
"People of Fúzhōu eat lychees,
and there is a moment of insight.
That's why I speak of this here."
This fellow practitioner in the monastic community
acts according to rules and walks the proper path,
without the faults of a monk.
It's a pity his measure is short.
Yet if he turns a somersault out,
he certainly won't be obscured.
There is an ancient saying,
which I present to the assembly:
The teachings say:
"When I do not see,
why do you not see the place where I do not see?
If you see the not-seeing,
naturally it is not that characteristic of not-seeing.
If you do not see the place of my not-seeing,
naturally it is not a thing.
How can it not be you?"
Later, Venerable Zhàntáng composed a verse:
"The old barbarian's thoroughgoing grandmotherly heart,
For Ānanda's sake, the meaning deepens further.
Hán Gàn's horse neighs at the grassy ferry,
Dài Sōng's ox rests in the shade of green willows."
Miàoxǐ also had a verse.
Though not very literary,
it is not below Zhàntáng's.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Shàoxīng reign period,
on the eleventh day of the third month,
at Dōngshān Temple in Xīngàn County of Línjiāng Commandery,
I received an imperial edict restoring my status as a monk.
After expressing gratitude for the imperial favor,
I took incense and offered prayers for the emperor.
Then I took my seat and said:
"The blue felt has always been our family's possession;
Today I return to being a monk as before.
How can such precious imperial grace be repaid?
By a vine upon the ten-thousand-year pine."
Then I raised my staff and said:
"The vine is right here.
But how shall we speak the phrase of repaying kindness?
If you can speak it,
'Even crushed bones and shattered body could not repay' - one phrase clearly transcends a hundred million. If not,
this mountain monk cannot but explain it for you all."
The officials of Xīngàn County.
Requested a general discourse.
A monk asked,
"The sage's grace has already been received,
The monastic form is once again complete.
This learner comes forward,
Begging the master to point out the renewed Dharma."
The master said,
"After rain, the stream's light is tranquil;
Clouds part, the mountain's colors are fresh."
The monk advanced,
"If so, then the dragon chart increases in lasting firmness,
The Buddha-sun turns with radiant light."
The master said,
"An old path of one way,
High and low naturally distinct."
The monk advanced,
"Just as when Dàdiān knocked his teeth,
Hán Wéngōng directly knew the return;
When Huángbò bestowed a name,
Minister Péi immediately knew the place.
I wonder, today when the venerable meets with the magistrate and court advisor,
What instruction is there?"
The master said,
"Two eyes facing two eyes."
The monk advanced,
"Is this not the instruction?"
The master said,
"Fully allowing to drill tortoise and strike tile."
The monk bowed.
The master then said,
"Asking is good, not asking is more intimate.
Why?
The path before sound—a thousand sages do not transmit it.
Learners toil in form like apes grasping at shadows.
Among them, if there is an heroic fellow,
Hearing this raised, immediately acts without hesitation,
Yet still remains in the vine's nest.
Only when inside there is nothing to realize, outside nothing to cultivate,
Like the earth holding up mountains,
Like stone containing jade,
Is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk lets go of body and life.
If one knows this,
Every dust, every thought is without emptiness or lack;
Bending, turning, bowing, lifting—all are within it.
Just at such a time,
After all, whose family's breeze and moonlight is it?
Do you thoroughly understand?
A thousand sages—where have they gone?
The long sword leaning against heaven chills people."
He further said,
"This is the magistrate and court advisor,
Today leading all fellow officials,
Together with resident worthy scholars and officials,
Coming together to rejoice in Zōnggǎo's tonsure,
Requesting the meaning of this passage of speaking the Dharma.
Questioning the Buddha has its cause;
Moreover, Zōnggǎo himself residing at Héngméi,
From beginning to end seventeen years,
Today unknowingly, unawares,
Comes once to Xīngàn,
Joining this Dharma assembly.
Is it not that in previous lives we were together at the Vulture Peak assembly as fellow Dharma listeners?
Originally, speaking the Dharma has its own time and place.
If the time, condition, and cause have not met,
Speaking the Dharma does not succeed.
Thus, Śākyamuni spoke the Dharma over three hundred sixty assemblies,
All establishing time and place.
What is meant by time and place?
Have you not seen,
At the end of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment it says:
Thus I have heard,
Once the Bhagavān,
Entered the samādhi of the great store of spiritual powers and great light,
This very one is today's time for speaking the Dharma.
Therefore it is said,
To understand the meaning of Buddha-nature,
One should observe the time and conditions.
When the time arrives,
The principle naturally manifests.
Have you not seen,
The Great Master Tiāntāi Zhìzhě, while reading the Lotus Sūtra,
Reached where the Medicine King Bodhisattva burned his body, saying:
'This is true vigor, this is called true Dharma offering to the Tathāgata,'
At this he suddenly understood,
The before and after were cut off,
And he realized the Lotus Samādhi.
In that samādhi, he saw the Vulture Peak assembly with Śākyamuni and the great multitude solemnly still gathered.
Now speaking of this to people,
If they have not entered such a state,
They absolutely will not believe.
Why?
Zhìzhě was from the Chén-Suí period, two thousand years after Śākyamuni,
How could it be that due to 'this is true vigor,
This is called true Dharma offering to the Tathāgata,'
Within the Lotus Samādhi,
He saw the Vulture Peak assembly solemnly still gathered?
Is this deceiving people?
Is it false speech?
This matter is known only through realization, difficult to fathom.
You should know that Miàoxǐ today speaking the Dharma,
Is no different from Śākyamuni speaking the Dharma at the Vulture Peak assembly.
No different from the Great Master Zhìzhě at Nányuè realizing 'this is true vigor, this is called true Dharma offering to the Tathāgata.'
Also no different.
Those who truly realize will certainly not deceive each other.
Those unrealized are like speaking of dreams.
Therefore it is said,
All past kalpas,
Placed in the future now;
Future present kalpas,
Returned to the past world.
Sealed by the Ocean-Reflection Samādhi with one seal,
Without any leakage,
No going, no coming, no before, no after.
Not only is Miàoxǐ one person thus,
The prefectural vice-minister is also thus.
Not only the prefectural vice-minister is thus,
The county magistrate, court advisor, fellow officials, and resident worthy scholars and officials are also thus.
Not only the county magistrate, court advisor, fellow officials, and resident worthy scholars and officials are thus,
Even those presently here, whether monastic or lay, noble or humble, are also thus.
Such a Dharma,
In heaven is one with heaven,
In humans is one with humans.
For those who should be saved by a Buddha's body,
It manifests a Buddha's body and speaks the Dharma.
For those who should be saved by an official's body, even a Brahmin or woman's body,
It manifests that body and speaks the Dharma.
This is the one-flavor pure, equal Dharma gate.
If here one understands,
Each person's original state, original face,
Then one knows the entire canon's 5,048 volumes, every phrase speaks of nothing else.
Impermanence is swift—do not treat it lightly.
Therefore it is said,
Strive in this life to finish it,
Do not let endless kalpas suffer further misery.
Human life is hard to obtain,
To be a noble person is even harder.
Have you not seen Śākyamuni's Sūtra of Forty-Two Chapters,
Inside which there are twenty difficulties?
Called: the poor giving alms is difficult,
The wealthy and noble learning the Way is difficult,
Having power yet not abusing it is difficult,
Among these there is 'risking life yet not dying is difficult.'
Do you all understand?
If one risks life, there is none who does not die,
How can one speak of the principle of not dying?
If you understand this,
Then only can you take the twenty difficulties,
Turn them over one by one,
All become easy matters.
Risking life yet not dying is also easy,
The poor giving alms is also easy,
The wealthy and noble learning the Way is also easy,
Having power yet not abusing it is also easy.
If awakened, then easy;
If not awakened, then difficult.
However, the two words 'difficult' and 'easy,'
Also do not concern the original state, the original face.
Why?
This Dharma gate originally has no difficulty, originally has no ease.
If able, at the place of neither difficult nor easy,
Urgently focus the eyes,
Externally cease all conditions, internally the mind without panting,
Then one knows the Dharma originally without difficulty or ease.
Nowadays, intelligent, sharp people,
Cannot immediately awaken.
Wherein lies the sickness?
Rather, because mind-consciousness acts first,
Obscured by mind-consciousness, one's own light is blocked,
The path is blocked,
Cannot advance.
Therefore here intelligence and sharpness are of no use.
One must internally not release, externally not admit.
Internally not releasing,
Is internally the mind without panting;
Externally not admitting,
Is externally ceasing all conditions.
When the internal mind is settled,
Then all conditions are also settled.
Therefore it is said,
The nāga is always in samādhi,
There is no time not in samādhi.
This great matter of cause and condition,
Is largely thus.
If able thus to believe, thus to understand,
Thus to cultivate, thus to realize,
Then the Buddhas of the three times are you all,
You all are the Buddhas of the three times.
No ancient, no modern,
The same liberation.
In the world, there is such a supreme matter,
Pity that the common people use it daily yet do not know.
However, today's assembly is also no small condition.
Moreover, bearing the various mountain Chan masters and all good men and faithful women,
Together here listening to the Dharma,
I humbly wish:
Hearing once, understanding a thousandfold, attaining the great dhāraṇī;
Once passing the ear-root, eternally becoming seeds of the Way.
Long standing, I humbly wish you take care.
Qián Jìyì requested a public discourse.
The Master said:
The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
If one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
then that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
not seeking the Dharma.
Since it is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
what then can be called the Dharma?
Reaching this point is like drinking water; one knows for oneself whether it is cold or warm.
Unless one personally verifies and awakens to it,
can one then see it.
If one is truly someone who has verified and awakened,
upon lifting a single fine hair,
the entire great earth becomes instantly clear.
Nowadays, not only Chan practitioners,
but even learned scholars who are intelligent, sharp, and exceedingly well-read,
each suffer from two kinds of ailments.
If they do not apply intention,
they become neglectful.
Neglectfulness causes them to fall into the ghost cave at the foot of the dark mountain.
In the teachings, this is called dullness and stagnation.
Applying intention leads to the mind-consciousness flying about in confusion.
One thought follows another,
the former thought not yet ceased, the latter thought already continuing.
In the teachings, this is called agitation and restlessness.
They do not know that beneath everyone's feet there is a great causal condition
that neither sinks nor agitates.
Like the sky universally covering,
like the earth universally upholding,
before the world existed,
this great causal condition was already present.
When the world disintegrates,
this great causal condition
remains unmoved by even a fine hair.
Often, scholars
mostly suffer from agitation.
Nowadays, in various places, there is a kind of erroneous silent illumination Chan,
which, seeing scholars obstructed by worldly toils and their minds unsettled,
conveniently teaches them to become cold ashes and withered trees,
to become a strip of white silk,
to become an incense burner in an old temple,
to go to a desolate, cold place.
Using this method to make people cease and rest—
tell me,
can they truly cease and rest?
They simply do not realize
that this monkey-mind,
if not dead, how can it cease and rest?
The one who goes forth as the vanguard and returns as the rearguard—
if not dead, how can it cease and rest?
This trend was extremely prevalent in Fújiàn circuit in previous years.
Miàoxǐ, in the early Shàoxīng period,
when he entered Mǐn and resided in a hermitage,
vigorously refuted it,
calling it the severance of the Buddha's wisdom life.
Even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, it cannot be repented.
Among them was a scholar named Zhèng Shàngmíng,
extremely intelligent, who understood the teachings,
understood the Daoist canon,
and was naturally versed in Confucianism.
One day, he came to Miàoxǐ's room holding a piece of incense,
his anger palpable,
his voice and expression severe.
He said: "Áng has a piece of incense not yet burned,
wishing to discuss a matter with the Reverend.
For instance, silent wordlessness
is the primary place of cessation and rest within the Dharma gate.
The Reverend recklessly slanders and criticizes it.
Áng suspects that the Reverend has not reached this state,
hence finds it hard to believe.
Consider how Śākyamuni, in the kingdom of Magadha,
for twenty-one days sealed himself in a room without uttering a sound—
was this not the Buddha's silence?
In Vaiśālī, thirty-two bodhisattvas
each explained the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Finally, Vimalakīrti remained silent,
and Mañjuśrī praised him, saying 'Excellent!'—
was this not the bodhisattva's silence?
Subhūti sat in meditation in the mountains,
wordless and speechless—
was this not the śrāvaka's silence?
When Śakra, lord of the devas, saw Subhūti sitting in meditation in the mountains,
he rained down flowers as an offering,
also without words or speech—
was this not the ordinary person's silence?
Bodhidharma traveled through Liáng and Wèi,
sat coldly at Shàolín for nine years—
was this not the Patriarch's silence?
Lǔzǔ, upon seeing a monk, would face the wall—
was this not the Chan Master's silence?
Reverend, for what reason
do you vigorously refute silent illumination,
considering it erroneous and wrong?"
Miàoxǐ said:
"Shàngmíng,
your question is fitting, wait and I will explain to you.
If my explanation is not valid,
then I will burn a stick of incense and bow to you three times.
If my explanation is valid,
then I will accept your incense burning and bowing.
I will not discuss for you the sayings of Śākyamuni or the virtuous elders of the past.
I will speak directly from within your own house.
As the saying goes, 'Borrow the old woman's skirt to bow to the old woman's age.'
Then he asked:
'Have you read the Zhuāngzǐ?'
He said: 'Why wouldn't I have read it?'
Miàoxǐ said:
'Zhuāngzǐ says:
"If words are sufficient,
then speaking all day exhausts the Dao;
if words are insufficient, speaking all day exhausts things.
The ultimate of Dao and things
cannot be fully conveyed by speech or silence.
What carries them is neither speech nor silence;
meaning has its ultimate."
I have not read Guō Xiàng's commentary or the annotations of various schools;
I will only, based on my own conjectural understanding, expose this silence of yours.
Have you not seen
how Confucius one day, greatly astonished, said:
"Shēn!
My Way is bound together with one thread."
Zēngzǐ replied: "Yes."
You scholars,
upon hearing this word "Yes,"
immediately come here speaking harshly, saying:
'This "Yes"

The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Similarity and difference disturb and confuse,
mutual dependence produces toil.
Long toil brings forth defilements, spontaneously becoming turbid.
From this arise defiled toils and afflictions,
movement creates the world,
stillness forms empty space.
Empty space represents similarity,
the world represents difference.
Where neither similarity nor difference exists,
truly conditioned dharmas arise.
Aware brightness and empty darkness
mutually depend and produce shaking.
Therefore, there is the wind wheel
that upholds the world.
From this we know
the world's formation is upheld by the wind wheel.
For the nature of wind is movement and shaking,
unceasing movement and shaking
suddenly produces solid obstruction.
Therefore it is said: because of emptiness, shaking arises;
solid brightness establishes obstruction.
That which is metal and treasure
is bright awareness establishing solidity.
Therefore, there is the metal wheel that preserves lands.
For wind and metal,
these two things rub against each other,
and from this, fire is produced.
Therefore it is said:
Solid awareness forms treasure;
shaking brightness produces wind.
Wind and metal rub against each other,
therefore there is the light of fire,
which has the nature of transformation.
Treasure brightness produces moisture,
firelight rises and steams,
therefore there is the water wheel
that contains the ten directions.
Fire rises, water descends,
mutually interacting, establishing solidity.
Moisture becomes the great oceans,
dryness becomes continents and sandbars.
For this reason,
in those great oceans,
firelight constantly arises.
On those continents and sandbars,
rivers constantly flow.
Where water's force is weaker than fire's,
it congeals into high mountains.
Therefore, when mountain rocks are struck, they become flame;
when melted, they become water.
Where earth's force is weaker than water's,
it sprouts as trees and plants.
Therefore, when forests encounter burning, they become earth;
when twisted, they become water.
Mutual delusions produce growth,
successively becoming seeds for each other.
Due to these causes and conditions,
the world continues.

it was as if only a single day had passed.
In upholding official duties and governance, he is never careless or simplistic,
handling all matters with leniency.
Incorruptible, cautious, and profoundly sincere,
he has never spoken of others' faults or wrongdoings.
This truly is the conduct practiced by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because he requested guidance using this scroll,
I therefore write these twenty-six passages for him.
It is also due to his pure sincerity and strong dedication to the Path.
I wish to support him in this,
so that he may practice according to these methods,
and in the future realize the great matter,
like eminent elders such as Yáng Dànián and Zhāng Wújìn,
to become protective Bodhisattvas within and without our tradition.
Then my words will not have been spoken in vain.
To learn this Way,
one should attend to the matter at one's own heels.
The moment there is the slightest involvement of intellectual understanding,
one immediately misses the message at one's heels.
When the message at one's heels is penetrated,
all kinds of intellectual understanding are none other than matters at one's heels.
Thus the ancestral teacher said:
When speaking directly of intellectual understanding,
intellectual understanding is precisely the mind.
The mind itself is intellectual understanding.
Intellectual understanding is right now.
If right now, without transcending a single thought,
toward one's heels,
one instantly extinguishes intellectual understanding,
then one can walk hand in hand with the ancestral teacher.
If one is not yet like this,
be careful not to cling to intellectual understanding.
When scholar-officials study the Way,
those with sharp faculties miss it,
while those with dull faculties find it difficult to enter.
Difficulty in entering causes them to retreat and give up on their own,
while missing it undoubtedly leads to slander.
If you wish to strike the middle,
simply take what is missed
and move it to the place of difficulty in entering,
then take what is difficult to enter
and move it to the place of missing.
Naturally, you will be tranquil,
no longer making interpretations about difficulty in entering or missing.
Having attained this,
it is good to then fully let go here.
When letting go, do not even make a principle of letting go.
As an ancient virtue said: "Roaming freely, always like a foolish simpleton,
in his own house, there naturally is one who understands and loves."
Also, Qīngliáng said:
"Expansive and unrestrained, let it come and go as it will,
in serene reflection, perceive its source and flow."
Speaking of verification, it cannot be shown to others;
speaking of principle, without verification it cannot be understood.
Nowadays, as soon as people hear such talk,
they think there really is such a matter,
and then say, "I am verified, I am awakened,"
yet cannot present it to others.
They always speak of lofty Chán,
seven verticals and eight horizontals,
talking nonsense and speaking recklessly,
deceiving spirits and frightening ghosts,
thinking that the matter of the ancestral teacher's school is only like this.
They do not realize
that what is personally verified and personally awakened
can only be known by those who are personally verified and personally awakened.
Without relying on words,
they naturally silently resonate with it.
Where they resonate, they also do not deliberately try to harmonize.
Like water entering water,
like gold exchanged for gold,
raising one clarifies three,
the eye discerns the slightest difference.
Only when reaching this state
can one speak of transcending the characteristics of speech,
transcending the characteristics of words,
transcending the characteristics of mental conditions.
It is not forced;
the Dharma is thus by nature.
In recent times in the monastic communities,
deviant teachings run rampant,
blinding the eyes of living beings
beyond count.
If we do not use the public cases of the ancients to raise awareness and pull along,
it is like a blind person letting go of the staff in hand:
not a single step can be taken.
Taking the circumstances of ancient virtues' entry into the Way,
they categorize them by type, saying:
"These cases are circumstances of the eye of the Way,
these are circumstances of penetrating sound and form,
these are circumstances of extinguishing emotions,"
and from the beginning, in order, case by case,
they speculate and measure,
discussing and deliberating on phrases.
Even if some recognize this illness,
they think that the Buddha-Dharma and the Chán Way
are not in written words and language,
so they dismiss everything and gulp down what is readily available,
after eating porridge and rice, sitting idly in a heap,
sitting in the ghost cave under the black mountain,
calling it "silent yet constantly illuminating,"
also calling it "like a greatly dead person,"
also calling it "the matter before parents were born,"
also calling it "the matter before the empty eon,"
also calling it "the message on the other side of威音,"
sitting and sitting,
sitting until calluses grow on their buttocks,
not daring to move,
calling it "the gradual maturation of effort."
Then they take many idle words and lengthy talk,
from the beginning, deliberating as principles,
transmitting and teaching once,
calling it the "essential purport."
Yet within their hearts, it remains pitch black.
Originally intending to eliminate self and others,
self and others become even higher;
originally intending to extinguish ignorance,
ignorance becomes even greater.
They do not realize
that this matter is only truly ultimate
when personally verified and personally awakened.
The moment there is even a single phrase or half-sentence interpreted as extraordinary, mysterious, secret, transmittable, or teachable,
it is not the true Dharma.
The true Dharma is neither transmitted nor taught;
only when I am verified and you are verified,
eye to eye relative,
mind to mind transmitted,
is the wisdom life of the Buddhas and ancestors continued unbroken.
Then, with what remains from applying to oneself,
one acts as a standard for beings.
Thus Dámó said:
"I originally came to this land,
to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings.
One flower opens five petals;
the fruit naturally ripens." This is it.
What is called transmitting the Dharma
is the mind Dharma.
The mind Dharma has no form or segment;
what is transmitted is as said before: "I am verified, you are verified."
If both sides are not verified,
and one seeks verification outside the mind, then there is an essential purport, mysterious and extraordinary, that can be transmitted and taught,
and then there is "I understand, you do not understand,"
giving rise to thoughts of contempt,
increasing the view of self.
The Thus-Come One says such people are pitiable.
In Miàoxǐ's Chán, there is no difference between difficult to investigate and easy to investigate.
It only requires the Chán investigator to cut off the path of birth and death before illness arises,
directly without doubting the Buddha, doubting the ancestors, doubting birth, or doubting death.
Difficult to investigate or easy to investigate
depends on the person;
it has nothing to do with Chán itself.
Often, clever and intelligent people
mostly seek quick results,
wanting something they can talk about with their mouths,
something they can rely on before them.
They do not realize
that those who attain this matter
are like a living lion turning and leaping;
in the person's daily activities throughout the twelve periods of the day,
like quicksilver falling to the ground,
large drops form large circles,
small drops form small circles,
without needing arrangement,
without relying on fabrication,
naturally lively and vibrant,
constantly revealed before you.
Precisely at such a time,
one first resonates with what Yīsùjué called: "Not seeing a single dharma is precisely Thus-Come, then one can be called observing freely."
If one is not yet like this,
temporarily set aside
this cleverness and reasoning,
and turn toward where there is nothing to grasp,
where there is no flavor,
and try to grasp and chew on it.
Grasping and grasping,
chewing and chewing,
suddenly, in the flavorless place, you bite your tongue;
in the place with nothing to grasp, you lose your nose.
Only then do you know why the old man Zhàozhōu said:
"Before leaving home, I was used by Bodhi;
after leaving home, I use Bodhi."
Sometimes picking up a blade of grass to make a sixteen-foot golden body,
sometimes taking the sixteen-foot golden body and turning it into a blade of grass.
Establishing is up to me,
sweeping away is up to me,
speaking principles is up to me,
not speaking principles is up to me.
I am the Dharma King,
free in the Dharma.
If I speak, there is much to say;
if I do not speak, there is nothing to say.
Having attained such freedom,
wherever I go, I am at ease.
The Sanskrit word "prajñā"
is translated here as "wisdom."
There has never been one who understood prajñā
yet had greed, anger, and delusion.
There has never been one who understood prajñā
yet harmed living beings.
Those who do such things
run counter to prajñā;
how can they be said to have wisdom?
Miàoxǐ often tells those within:
The moment you feel that in daily responding to conditions
is where effort is saved, that is where the person gains power.
Where power is gained saves limitless effort;
where effort is saved gains limitless power.
Often, when I have spoken too much about this,
it seems like people from Sìzhōu seeing the great sage:
they do not realize
that when Miàoxǐ speaks like this,
it is precisely the place of my ordinary practice.
Fearing there may be those who do not believe enough,
I cannot help repeatedly pulling along, raising awareness, dragging through mud and bringing water,
for having been a wanderer myself, I especially pity other wanderers.
The ancient sages,
never transmitted through words.
They only spoke of transmitting mind to mind.
Nowadays, most teachings rely on inherited interpretations.
This turns away from the original mind,
transmitting through language,
calling it the essential doctrine.
Those who act as teachers,
since their insight is already incorrect,
and learners lack resolute determination,
anxiously seeking to understand Chán,
striving to keep their mouths from being empty,
having something to say.
Wishing to attain open clarity of mind,
and reach the ultimate place of peace and bliss,
isn't this indeed difficult?
An ancient master said:
Words can cut off meaning.
Meaning can cut off words.
When meaning and words chase each other,
this is truly fearsome.
He also said:
In meaning, do not linger on words.
In words, do not linger on meaning.
As when Zhàoqìng asked Luóshān:
Venerable Yántóu said,
'Such, such,'
'Not such, not such.'
What is the meaning?
Luóshān then called, "Great Master!"
Zhàoqìng responded.
Shān said:
"Both bright and both dark."
Qìng then bowed and left.
After three days, he came again to ask:
"What was the meaning of your words the other day?"
Shān said:
"I have already told you everything."
Qìng said:
"Great Master is like one carrying fire."
Shān said:
"If so,
ask according to your doubt."
Qìng said:
"What is 'both bright and both dark'?"
Shān said:
"Born together, die together."
Qìng again bowed in thanks and left.
Later, another monk asked Luóshān:
"What about 'born together but not dying together'?"
Shān said:
"Like an ox without horns."
He asked again:
"What about 'born together and dying together'?"
Shān said:
"Like a tiger wearing horns."
To understand matters from of old,
one should always keep this story in mind.
Yet one must not deliberately force interpretations,
for forcing interpretations is wrong.
Do not cherish the extraordinary words and subtle phrases from various sources.
Each patriarch has his own teachings.
Those transmitted secretly in closed rooms,
or ancient public cases and the like—
such mixed poisons,
if stored in the storehouse consciousness,
will remain through kalpas and lifetimes, unable to escape the shore of birth and death.
Not only are they of no benefit,
but daily life is also obstructed by them.
The eye of wisdom cannot become clear and penetrating.
The ancients, compelled by necessity,
seeing that learners had many discriminative understandings and turned away from the path, clinging to words,
therefore used discriminative medicine
to treat your discriminative illnesses,
enabling your mind-ground to find peace and reach the state of non-discrimination.
Now you instead regard discriminative language as extraordinary,
mistaking the medicine for the disease.
Is this not lamentable?
An ancient sage said,
"The Buddha is the medicine for sentient beings.
When sentient beings are ill,
they use the medicine of no-sentient-beings illness.
Then the medicine turns back into illness,
worse than the original illness.
As previously stated,
the mixed poison that cannot be gathered up remains in the storehouse consciousness,
this is also what is meant here."
Amid the dust and toil of daily life,
the various unsatisfactory circumstances
are the sickness of sentient beings.
A single thought turning inward in reflection
is the medicine of the Buddha.
If one can, regarding the Buddha and sentient beings,
immediately cease generating distinctions,
then the sickness is cured and the medicine eliminated.
Only then does one begin to realize
what Páng Gōng meant by saying:
"In daily affairs, there is no distinction;
Only I myself harmonize spontaneously.
In everything, neither grasping nor rejecting;
Everywhere, avoid imposing contrivances."
When studying this path,
before finding an entry point,
it feels extremely difficult.
Hearing the master's instructions makes it seem even harder to comprehend.
This is because the mind seeking verification and rest has not been eliminated,
and instead becomes an obstacle itself.
Only when this mind finally rests,
does one realize it is neither difficult nor easy,
nor can it be transmitted by any teacher.
To be deluded and unaware of it
is a great mistake.
To cling to delusion while awaiting enlightenment
makes the mistake even greater.
Why is this?
It is because unawareness causes delusion.
Clinging to delusion while awaiting enlightenment
is to be unaware within unawareness,
deluded within delusion.
If you are determined to break through these two barriers,
please let go of everything at once.
If you cannot let go,
this cycle of delusion and enlightenment
will continue endlessly—when will it ever cease?
For those who cultivate the Way,
it is easier to empty external phenomena than to empty the mind in daily practice.
When phenomena are emptied but the mind remains unemptied,
the mind is overcome by phenomena.
Simply empty the mind, and phenomena will naturally become empty.
If the mind is already empty,
yet one gives rise to a second thought,
wanting to empty phenomena,
then this mind has not yet attained emptiness,
and is again seized by phenomena.
If this ailment is not eliminated,
there is no way to escape birth and death.
Have you not seen the verse presented by Páng Gōng to Mǎzǔ:
"Beings from all directions gather together,
each learning the practice of non-action.
This is the arena for selecting Buddhas—
return home with an empty mind and pass the examination."
Since this mind is already empty,
what thing outside the mind remains to be emptied?
Reflect upon this.
But if you attain the root, do not worry about the branches.
Emptiness of this mind is the root.
Once the root is attained, then all kinds of speech and all kinds of wisdom,
daily interactions and responding to circumstances as they arise,
in all their confusion and disorder,
whether joy or anger,
likes or dislikes,
favorable or adverse situations—
all these are but branches.
If in responding to circumstances you can maintain self-awareness,
then nothing is lacking and nothing is in excess.
The ancients would immediately use the stick or shout upon a student's entry.
They only feared that learners would not grasp it with sharp urgency.
How much less would they engage in tedious chattering,
discussing matters and principles,
or expounding on the profound and wondrous—
merely rolling around in the grass!
In recent years,
this Way has declined and weakened.
Those who occupy high seats as teachers
merely use the ancients' public cases,
either praising or criticizing them,
or transmitting them in secret chambers,
considering this to be the Chan Way.
Some take silent wordlessness
as the state before the empty kalpa beyond the sound of Vairocana,
considering this to be the Chan Way.
Some take what is seen with the eyes and heard with the ears, raising awareness and pulling at it,
considering this to be the Chan Way.
Some take wild and reckless actions, like striking a spark or a flash of lightning,
believing that once raised, it is understood,
and deny everything else,
considering this to be the Chan Way.
Since all these are incorrect,
then what is the true point of reliance?
If there were a true point of reliance,
how would it differ from these?
Those with discerning eyes will know as soon as it is raised.
This path has no limits.
The worldly toils are also without limits.
It merely depends on how one directs oneself in daily life.
Therefore, the Huáyán Sūtra states: In all worldly matters,
the mind should be like empty space, free from attachment.
Universally observe the true nature of all phenomena.
Arouse the great vow to eradicate the sufferings of sentient beings.
Never grow weary of or abandon the aspirations of the Mahāyāna.
Eliminate all views.
Cultivate the equal practices and vows of all Bodhisattvas.
What is called equal practices and vows
is also a mind without limits,
wherever directed, there is no obstruction or hindrance.
Learning worldly matters,
if one's effort is insufficient,
then one cannot succeed.
Learning the transcendental Dharma,
there is no place for your effort.
As soon as one intends to exert effort in seeking,
it becomes completely unrelated, thousands of miles away.
Although it is so,
having no place for effort,
no place to grasp,
no place to apply strength,
is precisely where one should apply strength.
Do not, upon hearing this said,
sprout branches beyond the section,
saying, "Since there is no effort, no grasping, no applying strength,
then how should one proceed?"
If one holds this view,
it becomes even more unrelated.
Impermanence is swift.
The matter of life and death is paramount.
Within the realm of sentient beings, affairs that follow the course of life and death
are as numerous as hemp and millet.
Having sorted them out once,
another batch arrives.
If one does not keep the words "life and death" right before the nose as a remedy,
then only when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives,
in frantic haste,
like a crab dropped into boiling soup,
will one realize regret—but by then it is too late.
If you wish to be direct and decisive,
please cut it off right now.
When learning worldly methods,
one must comprehend them clearly.
When learning otherworldly methods,
one must instead completely fail to comprehend them.
Only then is there potential for orientation.
Since one fails to comprehend them,
how then can one orient oneself?
Simply investigate in this manner.
The Buddha is the one within the realm of sentient beings who has settled matters.
Sentient beings are those within the realm of Buddhahood who have not settled matters.
To attain complete oneness,
simply let go of both Buddha and sentient beings
all at once.
Then there is neither settled nor unsettled.
Thus an ancient worthy said:
Just penetrate non-action in the midst of action,
and when seeing forms or hearing sounds, one need not be deaf.
A monk asked Zhàozhōu,
"Does the cypress tree have Buddha-nature or not?"
Zhàozhōu said, "It does."
The monk asked,
"When will it attain Buddhahood?"
Zhàozhōu said,
"Wait until empty space falls to the ground."
The monk asked,
"When will empty space fall to the ground?"
Zhàozhōu said,
"Wait until the cypress tree attains Buddhahood."
Considering these words,
do not think that the cypress tree will not attain Buddhahood,
nor that empty space will not fall to the ground.
After all, how is it?
When empty space falls to the ground,
the cypress tree attains Buddhahood.
When the cypress tree attains Buddhahood,
empty space falls to the ground.
You must contemplate this deeply.
The Buddha is a person free from affairs.
He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years.
According to the dispositions of sentient beings,
he prescribed remedies for their afflictions.
Through skillful means and ultimate truth, sudden and gradual approaches,
partial and complete, biased and perfect teachings,
he expounded the entire Tripitaka.
All are teachings free from affairs.
Since beginningless time,
sentient beings have been carried away by mind, intellect, and consciousness.
While being carried away, they remain completely unaware.
Thus, in the Prajñā assembly,
the Buddha taught the empty nature of all phenomena,
stating that eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects,
are all empty, merely having names.
At the ultimate point,
even names are empty.
Emptiness too cannot be grasped.
If a person possesses wholesome roots and predispositions from past lives,
they should focus on this ungraspable point,
letting mind, intellect, and consciousness die away,
then they will understand what old man Śākyamuni meant when he said:
"From the Deer Park initially,
to the Bhāgīrathī River finally,
during this entire period,
I have not spoken a single word."
These are words of truth.
Zen is not in stillness.
Not in clamor.
Not in the place of thinking and discrimination.
Not in the affairs of daily life and responding to conditions.
Yet even so,
above all, do not abandon stillness, clamor, daily activities, responding to conditions, or the place of thinking and discrimination to investigate—suddenly the eye opens,
and all are matters within your own house.
Nowadays, scholar-officials who study the Way
mostly advance half-heartedly and retreat half-heartedly.
When worldly affairs do not go as they wish,
they urgently seek to practice Chan meditation.
Suddenly, when worldly affairs go smoothly,
they then cease their practice.
This is because they lack resolute faith.
Chan is but another name for prajñā.
The Sanskrit term prajñā
is translated here as wisdom.
If a person lacks resolute faith
and also lacks wisdom,
yet wishes to transcend birth and death,
there is no possibility of this.
To learn this path,
one must possess resolute faith.
When encountering adverse or favorable circumstances,
the mind remains unshaken.
Only then is there potential for progress.
The Buddha said,
"Faith can eternally eradicate the root of afflictions,
faith can single-mindedly direct one toward the Buddha's virtues,
faith remains unattached to any state,
transcending all difficulties to attain freedom from hardship."
He further stated,
"Faith enables one to surpass the paths of demons,
revealing the unsurpassed way of liberation."
As clearly expounded in the teachings above,
how could the Buddha deceive people?
If one is half-enlightened and half-obscured,
half-believing and half-doubting,
then when encountering circumstances and conditions,
the mind gives rise to疑惑.
This is precisely because the mind becomes attached to states,
unable to develop absolute certainty in this path.
Eradicating the root of afflictions and transcending all difficulties
– these difficulties arise from lacking resolute faith,
being harassed by one's own skandha-demons.
If in one thought-moment one realizes dependent arising is unproduced, then without departing from this thought,
one immediately transcends the demonic paths.
The so-called demonic paths are nothing other
than obscuring this very mind,
deludedly generating various discriminative views outside this mind.
Thereupon this mind follows these deluded discriminative thoughts in continuous flow,
thus creating demonic states.
If one can directly and resolutely believe
that this mind is inherently and undoubtedly already Buddha, instantly abandoning all views,
then this very demonic path
becomes the individual's path to transcend birth-and-death and attain bodhi.
A practitioner of meditation,
when studying the scriptures and the stories of ancient masters' enlightenment,
must simply empty the mind.
Do not seek the profound or enlightenment through names, phrases, and meanings.
If such a thought arises,
it obstructs one's own correct knowledge and vision,
and for endless eons, there will be no entry point.
Pánshān said:
"It is like waving a sword in the air—
do not discuss whether it reaches or not,
yet do not neglect it."
Vimalakīrti said:
"The Dharma transcends the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
To penetrate this Dharma,
one must first remove the six sense faculties,
ensuring they have no faults.
What are the faults?
Being swayed by form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas,
unable to detach from them.
In the scriptures and the words of ancient masters,
seeking knowledge, views, or intellectual understanding is such a fault.
If one can, in studying the scriptures and the stories of ancient masters' enlightenment,
refrain from generating a second thought,
and directly realize the return,
then in one's own realm and others' realms,
all will be as wished,
all will be free and unhindered.
Déshān would strike as soon as a monk entered the gate;
Línjì would shout as soon as a monk entered the gate.
Eminent teachers everywhere
call this "confrontational guidance, direct transmission."
Miàoxǐ calls it "the highest form of dragging through mud and water."
Even if one fully embraces
the strike or shout,
they are not a true person of resolve
if they are drenched by a sudden bucket of foul water.
How much more so for those who,
beneath the strike or shout,
seek the extraordinary or profound understanding—
they are the most unawakened among the unawakened.
When the superior person hears the Way,
It is like a seal imprinting on emptiness.
When the average person hears the Way,
It is like a seal imprinting on water.
When the inferior person hears the Way,
It is like a seal imprinting on mud.
This seal and emptiness, water, and mud are without difference.
Because of the superior, average, and inferior persons,
There appears to be difference.
If now you wish to directly enter this Way,
Smash the seal completely,
Then come and meet Miàoxǐ.
The dusty toils of the burning house—
when will they ever end?
If one can attain peace and joy for a single day,
that becomes the model for ten thousand days.
Within a single day,
if the mind does not chase after things, does not indulge in false thoughts, and does not cling to any objects,
then it aligns with all the Buddhas of the three periods and all the great Bodhisattvas.
Without deliberate effort or contrivance,
it naturally becomes one whole.
The World-Honored One used the metaphor of the burning house
precisely for this reason.
The scripture says:
This house has only one gate,
and moreover it is narrow and small.
The children are young and immature,
not yet aware of anything,
attached to their play-place,
and may fall and be burned by the fire. I shall tell them of terrifying things.
This is fully detailed in the scripture.
This house has only one gate and moreover it is narrow and small—
this means the root of faith is narrow and inferior, within the burning house,
lacking wisdom and delighting in clinging to dusty toils.
It is because they do not believe there is a way out of the burning house to sit in the open ground, experiencing pure, wondrous joy.
But if within this state,
one can believe thoroughly and see through it,
not clinging to the childish play-place,
with a mind that does not chase, does not fantasize, and does not cling to objects,
then this very burning house with its dusty toils
becomes the place of liberation, transcending the three realms.
Why is this?
Did the Buddha not say?
Regarding all objects,
do not rely on them, do not dwell on them,
have no discrimination,
clearly see the Dharma-realm vast and peacefully established,
fully understand that all worlds and all dharmas are equal and non-dual.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva in the Far-Going Stage,
through the power of the wisdom they practice,
transcends all those of the Two Vehicles.
Although they attain the treasury of the Buddha's realm,
they manifest dwelling in the realm of demons.
Although they surpass the demonic path,
they display demonic methods.
Although they appear to practice like external paths,
they do not abandon the Buddha-Dharma.
Although they show conformity to all worldly ways,
they constantly practice all transcendent dharmas.
This is the true skillful means within the dusty toils of the burning house.
Those who study Prajñā,
if they abandon this skillful means
and instead follow along with dusty toils,
will certainly be seized by demons.
Moreover, within states of conformity,
if they forcibly expound principles,
saying that afflictions are precisely Bodhi,
that ignorance is precisely great wisdom,
while every step they take is in existence,
and every word they speak is about emptiness,
they themselves do not reproach the karma-power that pulls them,
and further teach others to deny cause and effect,
saying things like:
Drinking alcohol and eating meat do not hinder the practice of Bodhi; committing theft and sexual misconduct do not obstruct Prajñā.
Such types,
with evil demons and poisonous influences entering their heart and vitals,
remain completely unaware.
Wanting to escape dusty toils
is like trying to extinguish a fire by pouring oil on it—is this not lamentable?
The companions of dusty toils
are the seeds of the Tathāgata.
The teachings have clear text on this.
For example, on high, dry plateaus, lotus flowers do not grow;
it is in low, muddy wetlands that these flowers bloom.
Within the dusty toils of the burning house,
submerging and emerging,
suffering immeasurable pain,
suddenly within this suffering, one gives rise to weariness and detachment,
and begins to generate the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
The companions of dusty toils are the seeds of the Tathāgata—
this precisely refers to this.
Laypeople who study the Path
are vastly different
from those who have left home.
Those who have left home, from a young age, distance themselves from dusty toils;
their parents do not provide them with delicacies;
their six relatives are firmly abandoned and left behind;
their bodies dwell in pure monasteries;
their eyes behold the sapphire-blue forms and holy images;
thought after thought is on the Path;
mind after mind is uninterrupted.
The books they read
are none other than Buddhist books;
the things they do

Once the mental disposition is rectified,

Since he keeps the matter of birth and death in mind,

Once the mental disposition is rectified,

When events are harmonized with principle,

When effort is saved, that is where one gains strength in learning this path.
Where strength is gained, infinite effort is saved;

As soon as one dwells in the state of no speech,

As previously stated, poisonous snakes and fierce tigers can still be avoided,

In daily life, following conditions,

Raising it again and again,

Writing up to this point,

In recent times, many scholar-officials wish to learn this Way.

Once mixed toxins have entered their hearts,

Wherever they turn, they encounter obstructions,

Among recent scholar-officials,

When happy, when angry,
when judging public affairs,
when interacting with guests,
when gathering with wife and children,

Remember this well,
remember this well.
When worldly thoughts arise,
