This is the fifth example
used by ancestral teachers to help practitioners abandon wrong views and return to the right.
Miàomíng lay practitioner, just follow this in your investigation,
and in time you will naturally stumble upon realization.
The Dao is omnipresent.
Every encounter is genuine.
It is not established apart from genuineness.
Where it is established, there is genuineness.
As the teachings say, all livelihood activities accord with proper principle,
and do not contradict true reality.
Therefore, Páng Jūshì stated:
Daily affairs are no different,
Only I naturally harmonize.
In every matter, neither grasping nor rejecting,
In every situation, avoid contrivance.
Who assigns names to crimson and purple?
Mountains remain utterly free
from dust. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions—
carrying water and hauling firewood.
Yet if one merely clings to this
without seeking profound awakening,
one falls into the trap of idle passivity.
Have you not heard the words of the Elder Huáyán from Wèifǔ:
Buddhadharma lies precisely in your daily activities—
in walking, standing, sitting, reclining;
in drinking porridge, eating meals;
in verbal exchanges and inquiries.
But when it comes to all actions and every thought,
it is nevertheless not so.
Furthermore, Elder Zhēnjìng declared:
Without contrivance—each distinct yet marvelously subtle, each naturally genuine;
each like lotus blossoms unsullied by water.
Through confusion regarding one's own mind, one becomes a sentient being;
Through awakening to one's own mind, one attains Buddhahood.
Thus, sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas,
and Buddhas are fundamentally sentient beings.
It is due to confusion and awakening that distinctions arise.
Moreover, Śākyamuni proclaimed:
This Dharma abides in its Dharma position,
The appearances of the world are eternally abiding.
He further said:
This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptual discrimination.
This too is but another expression forbidding mental contrivance.
If, when responding to circumstances,
one neither arranges nor fabricates,
neither contrives thoughts nor discriminates and calculates,
then naturally one becomes vast and unimpeded—free from craving and attachments,
dwelling neither in the conditioned nor falling into the unconditioned,
entertaining no notions of worldly or transcendent.
This is the sixth manifestation
of not obscuring the original face
within the daily practice of the four dignified postures.
Originally, the matter of birth and death is grave, impermanence swift; one's own affairs not yet clarified.
Thus, one seeks out ancestral teachers to resolve the bonds of birth and death.
Yet, they are further entangled by ropes and cords added by misguided teachers.
Old bonds remain unsolved while new ones are added.
They pay no heed to the bonds of birth and death.
Instead, they only attend to idle chatter and lengthy discourses.
Calling it the essential teaching.
How utterly trivial and irrelevant.
In the teachings, this is called the error of misguided teachers.
It is not the fault of sentient beings.
To avoid being bound by birth and death,
Simply keep the mind constantly open and empty.
Just use the mind that knows not from whence it came nor where it goes,
And at all times, in response to conditions, maintain awareness.
When this awareness becomes familiar,
Over time, it will naturally become vast and unimpeded.
When you feel that daily practice requires less effort,
That is precisely where you gain strength in this path.
Gaining strength saves immeasurable effort.
Saving effort, in turn, yields immeasurable strength.
These principles
Cannot be spoken to others,
Cannot be shown to others.
The places of saving effort and gaining strength,
Are like drinking water—only you know if it's cold or warm.
Throughout his life, Miàoxǐ only pointed out to people where to save effort,
Not teaching them to make puzzles and speculate.
He himself practiced just like this.
Beyond this, there is no creating illusions or fabricating marvels.
Where I gain strength, others do not know.
Where I save effort, others also do not know.
When the mind of birth and death is extinguished, others do not know.
When the mind of birth and death is not yet forgotten, others also do not know.
Simply take this Dharma gate,
And bestow it upon all people.
There is no other mysterious or extraordinary secret to transmit.
If the lay practitioner Miàomíng is determined to practice like Miàoxǐ,
Then just follow these words.
There is no need to seek other principles externally.
Where the true dragon goes, clouds naturally follow.
Moreover, spiritual powers and light are originally inherent.
Have you not heard the words of Venerable Déshān:
"You simply have no affairs in the mind,
No mind in affairs,
Then empty yet luminous, void yet wondrous."
If you speak even a hair's breadth about origin and end,
It is all self-deception.
This is the essential path for those learning this Way,
The seventh model.
The above are seven examples.
The Buddha's afflictions, the Dharma's afflictions, and the afflictions of all sentient beings.
All spoken at once.
There is yet an eighth example.
Then I shall ask Miàoyuán Dàorén.
Again, on behalf of Miàoyuán Dàorén,
I offer a turning phrase:
For great matters, one cannot attend to small matters;
Miàomíng Jūshì must shoulder them himself.
The Buddha said:
If one wishes to know the Buddha's realm,
One should purify the mind like empty space.
Abandon deluded thoughts and all attachments,
Making the mind’s direction unobstructed.
With such determination to learn unsurpassed enlightenment,
Always keep the mind vast and empty.
Do not cling to words nor fall into empty silence.
Neither words nor silence—do not rely on either extreme.
Toward good and evil, neither grasp nor reject.
Throughout the twelve periods of day and night, cut off the calculating mind.
Do not dwell in emptiness, neither releasing inward nor admitting outward.
Like clouds in the sky, bubbles on water,
Suddenly appearing, suddenly vanishing.
Just here, turn over and cast aside, wiping clean the great void.
At such a moment,
It cannot be arranged,
Nor pieced together.
Why?
The great Dharma is originally thus.
It is not forced.
Have you not seen the words of old Śākyamuni:
“Do not grasp what sentient beings say;
All conditioned things are illusory.
Though not relying on the path of words,
Nor dwelling in wordless silence either.”
Nowadays, scholars studying this path,
Usually driven by clever intelligence,
Often seek principles in ancient sayings,
Trying to explain them clearly.
They do not realize
That on dried bones, surely no juice can be found.
Even if admonished by a good teacher
To transcend words and texts,
They sit instead in wordless silence,
Stuck in the dark cave of ghosts, unmoving.
To wish the mind’s direction unobstructed and unblocked—
Is that not difficult?
Since impermanence is swift and生死事大, with firm resolve,
Directly seek unsurpassed enlightenment.
All worldly illusory and unreal matters,
Set aside at once.
Then turn to where nothing can be grasped or rejected,
And gently observe:
Is there? Is not?
Until there’s nowhere to apply mind, nowhere to open mouth,
When the mind feels like a ball of hot iron,
Do not let go.
Just here, contemplate a critical phrase:
A monk asked Yúnmén,
“For killing father and mother, one repents before the Buddha.
Where does one repent for killing the Buddha and patriarchs?”
Yúnmén said: “Lù.”
If you have firm determination,
Just contemplate the word “lù.”
Transfer the mind that calculates worldly affairs
Onto the word “lù.”
Walking or sitting,
Use this “lù” to arouse awareness.
In daily interactions,
Whether joyful or angry,
Good or evil,
Serving elders or socializing with friends,
Reading sages’ classics and histories—
All are occasions for arousing awareness.
Suddenly, unknowingly,
On “lù,” all traces cease.
The teachings spoken by sages of the three traditions,
Need not be asked of others one by one;
Naturally, all becomes clear, everything manifests.
Did the Buddha not say:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with unobstructed wisdom,
Believe all worldly realms
Are the Tathāgata’s realm.”
An ancient worthy said:
“Entering the world, nothing remains beyond.”
This is the principle.
Only fear lacking firm faith and determination.
Without firm faith,
There will be regressing mind.
Without firm determination,
One cannot learn to the ultimate end.
And who has firm faith without regressing,
Firm determination reaching the ultimate?
Long ago, the second patriarch of Niútóu Mountain, Chán master Zhì Yán,
Was from Qǔ'ē,
Surname Huá.
In youth, his wisdom and courage surpassed others,
Height seven chǐ six cùn.
In Suí’s Dàyè era, he served as a lieutenant,
Often hanging a water filter on his bow,
Using it wherever he went.
Repeatedly followed generals in campaigns,
Frequently achieving military merits.
In Táng’s Wǔdé era,
Aged just forty,
He requested to leave home,
Entered Shūzhōu’s Wǎngōng Mountain,
Became a disciple of Chán master Bǎoyuè.
One day while sitting peacefully,
He saw a extraordinary monk over ten chǐ tall,
With majestic bearing,
Clear and bright speech,
Who told Yán:
“You, in your eightieth life leaving home,
Should intensify diligence.”
After speaking, he vanished.
Once, while meditating in a valley,
Mountain waters flooded,
Yán sat peacefully unmoved,
And the waters receded on their own.
A hunter passing by,
Thereby reformed and cultivated goodness.
Also, two former comrades from the army,
Hearing Yán had secluded himself,
Went together into the mountains to find him. Seeing him, they said:
“Lieutenant, are you mad?
Why dwell here?”
Yán replied:
“My madness is awakening;
Your madness is just erupting.
Indulging in desires, fame, and favor,
Revolving in birth and death—
How can you free yourselves?”
The two, awakened and sighing, departed.
In Zhēnguàn era, he returned to Jiànyè,
Entered Niútóu Mountain, visited Chán master Lǎn Róng,
And realized the great matter.
Lǎn Róng told Yán:
“I received the true instruction from Great Master Xìn,
All attainments vanished.
If there were a dharma beyond nirvāṇa,
I’d say it’s like a dream too.
One dust speck flies and obscures the sky;
One mustard seed falls and covers the earth.
You have now passed this view;
What more can I say?
The guidance of this mountain gate,
I entrust to you.”
Thus he became Niútóu’s second patriarch.
This is having firm faith without regressing,
Firm determination reaching the ultimate—an example.
The teachings spoken by sages of the three traditions,
All advise goodness, warn against evil, rectify the mind.
If the mind is not upright,
Then treachery pursues only profit.
If the mind is upright,
Then loyalty and righteousness follow only principle.
Principle here means moral principle,
Not just conceptual reasoning.
Like your honored father the commissioner,
Seeing duty, he acts,
Displaying extraordinary true courage—
This is that principle.
Guīfēng Chán master said:
“Doing righteous deeds is an awakened mind;
Doing unrighteous deeds is a deluded mind.
Delusion follows emotions;
At death, one is pulled by karma.
Awakening doesn’t follow emotions;
At death, one can transform karma.”
This too is that principle.
The Buddha said: “In principle, sudden enlightenment—all delusions vanish at once;
In practice, gradual elimination—ended step by step.”
This too is that principle.
Elder Lǐ said:
“Perfect harmony doesn’t hinder sequential order;
One is many.
Sequential order doesn’t hinder perfect harmony;
Many are one.”
This too is that principle.
Yǒngjiā said:
“One ground contains all grounds;
One dharma fully includes all dharmas.
One moon universally reflects in all waters;
All water-moons are gathered in one moon.”
This too is that principle.
The Huáyán says:
“Buddha-dharma and worldly dharma,
If seen in their reality,
All are without difference.”
This too is that principle.
The difference lies in people, not in the dharma.
Loyalty and treachery are born with one.
The loyal among the treacherous
Are like a pure maṇi jewel placed in mud—
Even for ages, it cannot be defiled.
Why?
Its nature is inherently pure.
The treacherous among the loyal
Are like poison placed in a clean vessel—
Even for ages, it cannot change.
Why?
Its nature is inherently turbid.
As said before, difference lies in people, not in the dharma—
This is that principle.
Like two people, treacherous and loyal,
Reading the same sage’s books.
The sage’s books are the dharma,
Originally no difference.
But the treacherous and loyal reading them
Understand according to their kind—
Thus there is difference.
Vimalakīrti said:
“The Buddha preaches dharma with one sound;
Sentient beings understand each according to their kind.”
The loyal, seeing duty,
Their nature emerges.
The treacherous, seeing profit,
Their nature emerges.
Like a magnet meeting iron,
Or fire meeting dry tinder,
Even if one tries to restrain it,
It cannot be done.
Like your honored father the commissioner,
Heroic and fierce, surpassing others,
Proclaiming great duty amid thousands,
Stirring the times—also his loyal nature,
Seeing duty, it emerges,
Not fabricated, not arranged.
As the teachings say: “Like a mighty nāga warrior,
If fiercely angered,
On his forehead boils will arise.
Before they heal, none in Jambudvīpa can subdue him.”
The Buddha used this to比喻 those arousing bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta is the loyal mind.
Names differ, essence same.
When this mind encounters duty,
Then worldly and beyond,
All are accomplished at once,
Nothing lacking, nothing extra.
Though I am a Buddhist,
My heart loving the ruler and worrying for the country
Equals that of loyal scholars.
But my strength falls short,
And years pass by.
My will to love right and hate evil,
Is born with me.
As Yǒngjiā said: “Even if an iron wheel spins on my head, my samādhi-prajñā remains undiminished.”
Though I am not sharp,
I dare directly trust without doubt.
Jìgōng, your aspirations are extraordinary,
In the prime of life,
Just when busy with worldly toils,
Yet able now to return
And learn unsurpassed enlightenment—
Without past planted roots of virtue,
How could you trust firmly, hold steady, be master?
May you strengthen this mind,
Consistent from start to end.
Meeting situations and conditions,
Unchanging, unmoving,
Then called a person of great power.
Impermanence is swift,生死事大.
If every thought considers this great cause,
As unfinished, unspoken,
Directly transcending to realization,
You’ll save much obstructive evil karma in daily interactions.
How much more when one thought corresponds, turning ordinary to sage?
Just bring forth the willing heart,
Surely you won’t be misled.
Since ancient times, there are models of goodness.
Studying all books extensively, just know where the sages directed their minds.
Knowing that, your own mind becomes upright.
Mind upright, then all poisons and heresies
Cannot defile you.
Jìgōng, determined to learn Confucianism,
Must expand and fulfill it,
Then extend the surplus to benefit others.
Why?
Learning not reaching the end is not learning.
Learning reached but not applicable
Is not learning.
Learning unable to transform others
Is not learning.
Learning to the ultimate end,
Literature is therein,
Martial arts are therein,
Affairs are therein,
Principle is therein.
Loyalty, filial piety, even self-cultivation, governing people, pacifying states—all arts
Are therein.
Old Śākyamuni said:
“Always herein,
Walking, standing, sitting, lying.”
This is that message.
None are loyal to the ruler yet unfilial to parents;
None are filial to parents yet disloyal to the ruler.
But what sages praise, follow and practice;
What sages condemn, dare not violate.
Then in loyalty, filiality, affairs, principle,
Self-cultivation, governing people—all are encompassed,
All are clear.
Soon we’ll see your honored father the commissioner
Establish great merit and return victorious;
Jìgōng soaring to the azure clouds above,
The Chéng family
Having both martial and literary
Is beyond doubt.
Jìgōng, strive on.
Learning and pursuing the Way are one and the same.
In learning, one may not yet have reached the level of a sage,
but aims to inevitably attain it.
In pursuing the Way, one seeks to recover the lost mind amidst things and self,
where things and self become one.
Then both the Way and learning are fully equipped.
Scholars and officials extensively study all books,
not solely for self-cultivation, seeking wealth and honor, or pursuing pleasure.
When both the Way and learning are possessed and expanded upon,
then, beyond fulfilling oneself,
one can extend to others.
Modern scholars
often abandon the root for the branches,
turn away from the right to embrace the wrong,
using learning and the Way merely as names,
focusing solely on gaining wealth and honor and expanding their influence
as their definitive purpose.
Thus, their mental disposition is not upright,
and they are swayed by external things.
As the common saying goes, they only see the sharpness of the awl's tip,
but fail to see the squareness of the chisel's head.
They do not realize
that in Confucianism, rectifying the mental disposition comes first.
Once the mental disposition is rectified,
then even in haste or adversity, it aligns with this Way.
This is the meaning of learning and the Way being one, as mentioned before.
In our teaching, it is said:
If one can transform things, one is like the Tathāgata.
In Laozi's teaching, it is called compassion and frugality,
and not daring to be first in the world.
If one learns in this way,
there is no need to seek conformity with this Way,
for naturally and silently, one aligns with it.
The Buddha taught all dharmas
to save all minds.
If I have no mind to save,
what use are all dharmas?
It should be known that reading scriptures and studying teachings,
extensively exploring all books,
is like seeing the moon and forgetting the finger,
catching the fish and forgetting the trap,
as the primary meaning.
Then one is not swayed by words and language,
but can instead master words and language.
Have you not heard of the monk who once asked Guīzōng the monk,
"How can a beginner find an entry point?"
Guīzōng tapped the lid of the tripod three times with fire tongs and said,
"Do you hear it?"
The monk said, "I hear."
Guīzōng said,
"Why do I not hear?"
Guīzōng tapped three times again and asked,
"Do you hear it?"
The monk said, "I do not hear."
Guīzōng said,
"Why do I hear?"
The monk was speechless.
Guīzōng said,
"Guānyīn's wondrous power
can save the world from suffering."
Friend Rùnfǔ, you have long planted virtuous roots,
and believe in this great cause and condition,
with continuous mindfulness without interruption.
Yet, in all words and language,
you have not yet reached the stage of seeing the moon and forgetting the finger, or catching the fish and forgetting the trap.
If you can grasp Guīzōng's instruction,
then you will understand Guānyīn's enlightenment of perfect penetration,
and the meaning of Guīzōng's hearing and not hearing,
as non-dual and indistinguishable.
How can we know this is so?
Initially, in hearing,
one enters the stream and forgets the object.
When the object entered is silenced,
the two aspects of movement and stillness
clearly do not arise.
If the aspect of movement does not arise,
then the world's phenomena of birth and cessation cease.
If the aspect of stillness does not arise,
then one is not bound by cessation and extinction.
If, between these two, one does not dwell in the aspect of movement,
nor is trapped by the aspect of stillness,
then, as Guānyīn said, when birth and cessation cease, cessation and extinction appear.
Upon reaching this state,
one attains the oneness of body and mind, with nothing beyond the body.
Everything becomes clear, and all things are revealed.
This is not forced;
it is the nature of the dharma.
Rùnfǔ, strive diligently.
The Thirteenth Patriarch Jiāpímóluó
visited the Fourteenth Patriarch Lóngshù in a mountain cave.
Lóngshù knew of his coming in advance
and immediately went out to greet him.
As soon as they met, he said:
"Deep mountains and solitary desolation are where dragons and pythons dwell.
Venerable One of supreme virtue, why trouble your divine steps?"
Móluó replied:
"I am not one of supreme virtue,
but have come to visit the worthy one."
Lóngshù silently contemplated:
"Has this master attained the decisive nature and illuminating path-eye?
Is he a great sage who will inherit the true vehicle?"
Móluó said:
"Although you spoke in your mind,
I have already understood your intent.
Simply resolve to leave home—
why doubt my sagehood?"
Upon hearing this instruction,
Lóngshù immediately took ordination.
Since ancient times, venerable masters sought people through the Dharma.
When teachers were superior and disciples strong,
plucking the string distinguished the tune.
Every word, every phrase, every utterance, every silence
was never applied in vain.
This can be called mind and eye mutually illuminating, like glue and lacquer uniting.
Nowadays it is not so.
Those who serve as teachers
spend entire years
entangled in convolutions with learners,
yet never know whether they have arrived or not, understood or not.
Learners likewise cannot distinguish whether their teacher is deviant or correct.
This is because beginners' minds are coarse and teachers' instructions reckless.
Thus the authentic tradition becomes insipid,
while deviant methods proliferate wildly.
Such individuals
wishing to repay the immense kindness of former virtues—
what is called illuminating the path-eye and inheriting the true vehicle—
is this not difficult indeed?
Participating in Chan and studying the Way is for no other purpose
than to have this plot of land
with its boundaries and divisions
thoroughly clear
when the eye-light falls to the ground on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month.
It is not for engaging in conversation pieces or frivolous debates.
In recent times, this path has become desolate.
Teachers and disciples do not trust each other.
They must rely on scraps of old paper sprinkled with venom,
worthless and impure, given to learners
and called "Chan gatherings."
Bitter, bitter indeed!
Our Way is lost!
Have you not seen how in former times, the Venerable Línjì took leave of Huángbò?
Huángbò asked:
"Where are you going?"
Línjì replied:
"If not south of the river, then north of the river."
Huángbò immediately struck him.
Línjì caught the staff and gave him a slap.
Huángbò laughed heartily,
calling to the attendant: "Bring here the meditation board of our former teacher Bǎizhàng."
Línjì also summoned the attendant:
"Bring fire!"
Huángbò said:
"Just take it with you.
Hereafter you will seat yourself above all people under heaven—
your tongue is secure."
Later, Wéishān brought up this dialogue and asked Yǎngshān:
"Did Línjì perhaps fail Huángbò?"
Yǎngshān said: "Not so."
Wéishān asked:
"What is your understanding?"
Yǎngshān replied:
"Only those who know kindness can repay kindness."
Observe these transcendent individuals—
casually revealing traces of a different breed
already sets them apart from ordinary people.
Later, Línjì indeed propagated the essential teaching of Jiāngxī north of the river.
This is what is called: "The trampling of dragon-elephants cannot be endured by donkeys."
Zūnpǔ, a Chan practitioner,
once attended to Teacher Yuánwù at Jiǎngshān.
He and Elder Xiángyún Tányì were companions on the path.
Both studied under the teacher,
yet were satisfied with minimal attainment,
tapping their chests in self-assurance,
their nostrils turned skyward in arrogance,
believing none in the world surpassed them.
In the spring of Jiǎyǐn year,
I came to Mǐn from Jiāngzuǒ.
Tányì was already teaching in Púzhōng,
drawing crowds of monks with his滔滔 rhetoric.
Zūnpǔ followed him,
mutually reinforcing each other.
Knowing their understanding was unstable,
I feared they would mislead learners,
so I sent a letter to Tányì,
urging him to take leave and come temporarily.
Tányì, fearing loss of reputation,
delayed his departure.
Thus during a small assembly,
I severely criticized his errors,
posting a notice at the gate,
informing the fourfold assembly.
Hearing this, Tányì had no choice but to break retreat and come.
When questioned about his realization,
it remained just as before,
with no difference whatsoever.
I spoke to him with utmost sincerity:
"With such views as yours,
how dare you claim succession from Old Man Yuánwù?
If you truly wish to fully understand this matter,
then resign from the monastery and come."
Tányì said,
"I will return to the hermitage by summer's end."
True to his word,
he and Zūnpǔ came together.
Both entered the room,
yet for a long time failed to grasp the reality.
One day I asked Zūnpǔ:
"Regarding the dialogue about Sānshèng and Xìnghuà appearing or not appearing, helping others or not helping others—
tell me,
do these two old fellows have an escape route?"
Zūnpǔ struck my knee with a fist.
I said:
"Was that punch for Sānshèng's sake,
or for Xìnghuà's?
Speak quickly, quickly!"
As Zūnpǔ hesitated,
I struck his back with a stick.
Then I told him:
"You must never forget this stick blow!" For a long time he didn't understand.
One day while listening to another monk's interview,
I asked the monk:
"Déshān would strike as soon as a monk entered;
Línjì would shout as soon as a monk entered;
Xuěfēng would ask 'What is it?' as soon as a monk entered;
Mùzhōu would say 'The ready-made case—I'll give you thirty blows!' as soon as a monk entered.
Tell me,
these four old fellows—
did they have a way of helping others?"
The monk said, "Yes."
I said, "Stab!"
As the monk hesitated,
I immediately shouted him out.
Hearing this, Zūnpǔ suddenly broke through,
casting off all previous wrong knowledge and understanding.
Now he has become a truly free monk,
though his upward-looking eye is not yet fully open,
he clearly understands the matters from of old,
indeed without limit.
This is truly delightful.
Tányì also subsequently,
with a single word,
gained solid footing.
Now both are courageous and sharp,
advancing forward, finally understanding my usual concern lies not in worldly matters.
After the Lantern Festival in Yǐmǎo year,
Zūnpǔ came to request leave,
to return to Chángxī to visit his mother,
and asked for Dharma words, so I casually wrote these previous accounts for him.
At Jiànshàn there is Fóyǎn和尚's foremost Dharma-successor, Old Man Cángliù.
That venerable one—
scolds Buddhas and curses patriarchs,
possessing the eye for selecting Dharma,
no less than Old Páng.
Try showing this to him—
he will certainly offer critique.
Also request this elder to serve as witness.
Return before summer
to fully resolve the final great matter of causation.
Don't let the weight sink into the well!
Among fellow practitioners, though separated by千里, the wind blows the same—
Master Dìngguāng Miàodào asked Yúnmén,
"Regarding this mind and this nature, how do delusion and enlightenment, alignment and opposition, relate?
I beg for instruction at the essential point."
Yúnmén remained silent for a long time without answering.
Miàodào asked again.
Yúnmén laughed and said,
"If we speak of the essential point,
then it cannot be indicated to others.
If it could be indicated,
then it would not be essential."
Miàodào said,
"Is there no expedient means to guide learners toward it?"
Yúnmén said,
"If we speak of expedient means, then mind has no delusion or enlightenment,
nature has no alignment or opposition.
But people establish delusion and enlightenment,
perceive and cling to alignment and opposition.
Trying to understand this mind and see this nature,
this very mind and this very nature
then follow people's inversions and confusions, flowing into erroneous paths.
Thus, Buddhas and demons become indistinguishable,
wrong and right become inseparable.
This is because they fail to realize that this mind and this nature are like illusions, falsely establishing two kinds of names and concepts,
taking alignment/opposition and delusion/enlightenment as real,
recognizing this mind and this nature as true, not knowing that
whether real or unreal,
whether false or not false,
worldly and transcendental are merely provisional speech.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
'The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, perceived, or known.
If you practice seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing,
this is seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing,
not seeking the Dharma.'
Also, an ancient virtue said:
'If you take your own self-mind as ultimate,
there must be other things and other people as antidotes.'
Also, Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
'You take form and emptiness as mutually opposing and contending within the Tathāgatagarbha,
and the Tathāgatagarbha follows as form and emptiness pervading the dharma realm.
I use the wondrous brightness, neither ceasing nor arising, merging with the Tathāgatagarbha,
and the Tathāgatagarbha is only wondrous awareness illuminating and universally shining upon the dharma realm.'
The Tathāgatagarbha is this mind and this nature.
And the Buddha provisionally indicated that form and emptiness mutually opposing and contending is wrong,
while the wondrous brightness neither ceasing nor arising is right.
These two passages are medicinal words,
curing the two illnesses of delusion and enlightenment.
They are not the Buddha's fixed meaning.
They are words to break the clinging to delusion/enlightenment, mind/nature, alignment/opposition as real dharmas.
Have you not seen Bodhisattva Vajragarbha say:
'All three times are only speech.
All dharmas have no basis in speech.
All speech has no basis in dharmas.'
If delusion/enlightenment views perish and alignment/opposition understanding ceases,
then this mind becomes clear and bright like the bright sun,
this nature becomes vast and expansive equal to empty space.
Right under your feet, light shines and earth trembles, illuminating the ten directions.
Those who see this light all realize the patient acceptance of non-arising.
When you reach such a state, naturally you silently merge with this mind and this nature.
Only then do you know that originally there was no delusion, now there is no enlightenment.
Enlightenment is delusion, delusion is enlightenment.
Alignment is opposition, opposition is alignment.
Nature is mind, mind is nature.
Buddha is demon, demon is Buddha.
One path, pure and equal,
without equal or unequal.
All are the constant aspects of our mind,
not relying on other methods.
Even having attained this,
it is still speaking out of necessity.
You cannot take it as real.
If you take it as real,
then again you don't understand expedient means,
fixating on dead words, increasing falsehood,
revolving in confusion without end.
Reaching here, there is no place for you to apply your mind.
Better to know such matters,
set them aside,
then turn your head and look:
Mǎzǔ's 'mind itself is Buddha',
'not mind, not Buddha',
'not mind, not Buddha, not thing';
Zhàozhōu's 'cypress tree in the courtyard';
Yúnmén's 'Mount Sumeru';
Dàyú's 'sawing a scale weight';
Venerable Yányáng's 'clod of earth';
Fényáng's 'don't have false thoughts';
Jùzhī's 'raising a finger';
after all, what principle is this?
This is Yúnmén's expedient means.
Miàodào, ponder this.
The Way cannot be learned.
What is acquired through learning is not genuine attainment.
Yet the Way cannot remain unlearned.
Without learning, there is no hope of attainment either.
Learning or not learning, attaining or not attaining—
these have absolutely nothing to do with this Way.
I urge you to summon your vital energy
and make a complete turn right where there is no connection.
Then the mind that learns becomes the mind that does not learn,
the mind that attains becomes the mind that does not attain.
Like hot water melting snow,
you will finally realize that all previous disturbances
were actually your own close kin,
completely unrelated to those idle spirits and wild ghosts.
This is why Mùzhōu, the moment he saw a monk enter the gate,
would say:
"Here's a ready-made case—I'll give you thirty blows!"
And Zhàozhōu, when he saw a monk enter,
would say:
"You've let this old monk down."
These two elders were like the golden-winged peng bird splitting the ocean to directly seize and swallow the dragon.
How can the confused masses deliberate on this?
How can they approach it?
Is there any principle here for helping others?
You must not hear such teaching and then just rest and cease there.
Can you truly cease?
The ancients condemned this as the heterodox soul fallen into empty annihilation,
the unperishing dead person.
If you wish to be directly free of affairs,
simply at the place where it cannot be learned,
try to take one step forward and see.
If you can take this step,
then the Three Vehicles and twelve divisions of scriptures,
all the old masters under heaven speaking horizontally,
vertically, directly, or circuitously,
in praise or in criticism,
in conventional terms or in explicit revelation—
what are they but the sound of a hot bowl ringing?
Chán practitioner Yán, can you trust this? Do not just memorize my words.
Long ago, the monk Língyún saw peach blossoms
and suddenly attained enlightenment.
He composed a verse saying:
"For thirty years I've sought the sword-wielder,
How many times have leaves fallen and branches sprouted anew?
Since once laying eyes on the peach blossoms,
Up to this very moment, I've had no further doubts."
Monk Wéishān questioned him about his realization,
finding it in complete accord [with the truth],
and thus certified him, saying:
"What is attained through conditions
will never regress or be lost."
Furthermore, Monk Xuěfēng wrote in the preface to his own stupa inscription:
"That which arises from conditions
forms and decays from beginning to end.
What is not obtained through conditions
remains firm throughout the ages."
Now, regarding the insights of these two venerable masters,
tell me: are they the same or different?
If you say they are the same,
one affirms attainment through conditions as right,
while the other denies attainment through conditions as wrong.
If you say they are different,
we cannot have two great elders establishing separate schools and confusing later generations.
The goose king selecting milk was never like the duck.
Zhi Lì, practitioner of Chan, do you know where these two great elders stand?
If you do not know,
Yúnmén will plainly explain it for you:
"Two arise from one, but do not cling to the one either.
When the one mind does not arise, all dharmas are blameless."
The above two passages differ,
but both are included in the previous section○.
A monk practicing Chan meditation
must clarify the mind-ground.
A scholar studying for the imperial exams must attain success.
If one reads five cartloads of books yet fails the exams,
they remain merely a scholar for life.
To call them an official would be mistaken.
If a monk practicing Chan fails to clarify the mind-ground,
they cannot resolve the great matter of birth and death.
They remain merely an ordinary mortal for life.
To call them a Buddha would be mistaken.
Just these two errors
truly have such reality,
yet truly lack such reality.
Speaking of true existence: scholars
who pass exams and become officials
are seen constantly.
Speaking of true non-existence: Chan practitioners becoming Buddhas have never been witnessed.
Exchanging this for that,
it's six of one and half a dozen of the other.
This teaching is extremely simple yet profoundly far-reaching.
Often, learners
with a mind seeking attainment
approach the place where nothing is attained,
falling into pits and stumbling into ditches frequently.
Thus Yúnmén's words become empty talk.
Truly, like ghee's exquisite flavor treasured by the world,
encountering such people, it instead becomes poison.
Long ago, Chánshī Zhìcháng went to Cáoxī to see the Patriarch,
relating the essential mind teaching revealed by Hétong Dàshī.
The Patriarch, addressing his doubts,
spoke a verse saying:
"Not seeing any dharma yet maintaining 'no-seeing'
is greatly like floating clouds obscering the sun's face.
Not knowing any dharma yet clinging to 'empty knowledge'
is just as the great void producing lightning.
When such knowledge and views suddenly arise,
mistaken recognition has never understood skillful means.
You should in one thought know your own errors,
your own spiritual light constantly manifesting."
Zhìcháng, hearing the verse, immediately resolved his doubts and experienced great awakening.
The Patriarch's skillful means
led him to compose a verse presented to the Patriarch, ending:
"Had I not entered the Patriarch's room,
I'd be茫然 lost between two extremes."
Wondrous explanation! Chan practitioners, do you know the place where "truly having such reality" and "truly lacking such reality" land?
Don't concern yourself with ordinary mortals and Buddhas, scholars and officials.
Just recognize Yúnmén's skillful means.
If you can recognize this, going to Cháoyáng,
Cáoxī is not far.
But if not yet so,
under your feet, take care of Dàdiān Heshang.
Discerning the eyes of dragons and snakes,
seizing the opportunity against tigers and rhinos.
Unless one is a person who transcends measurements and is not bound by worldly ties,
this teaching will be regarded as mere idle talk.
Thus, the Linji school's style is difficult to inherit.
In recent times, those who learn through words
often compete in sharpness and flaunt their speech,
delighting in reckless talk and chaotic doctrines as if wielding freely,
treating arbitrary shouts and random yells as the essence.
With each push and pressure,
like striking sparks from flint,
resembling flashes of lightning,
before one can deliberate,
they burst into loud laughter,
claiming it to be swift and sharp insight, untainted by conceptual thought.
Yet they fail to realize
that this is precisely the deluded consciousness playing tricks with ghostly eyes.
Is it not deceiving themselves and misleading others?
Consider when Linji was attending Deshan:
Deshan turned and said,
"May I ask you something?"
Linji replied,
"Why is the old man talking in his sleep?"
As Deshan made to grab his staff,
Linji overturned the meditation seat.
Deshan then let it rest.
Now, tell me, in such spirited exchanges between these two elders,
is there any room for deliberation?
Truly, the trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure.
Without genuinely possessing such vision and such application,
one inevitably gets caught in weighing gains and losses, speculating and calculating.
Again, when Linji and Puhua were in Zhenzhou,
attending a lay donor's meal offering,
Linji asked, "The vast ocean swallowed in a hair, Mount Sumeru contained in a mustard seed—
is this the marvel of spiritual powers,
or is it thus by nature?"
Puhua promptly kicked over the meal table.
Linji said,
"Too crude!"
Puhua retorted,
"What kind of place is this?
To speak of crude or fine?"
Linji let it rest.
The next day, they attended another donor's meal together.
Linji asked again,
"How does today's offering compare to yesterday's?"
Puhua again kicked over the meal table.
Linji said, "It is so, but
too crude!"
Puhua said,
"Blind man! In the Dharma, what do crude and fine mean?"
Linji again let it rest.
Now, tell me, when Linji twice let it rest, was there any room for deliberation?
If so, how would one deliberate?
Chan practitioner Chongmi has long dwelled in the monastic community,
often able to deliberate, explain, and critique,
believing himself to have fully comprehended everything.
Later, he realized his error,
and at once set it all aside,
applying effort where no deliberation is possible.
Only now does he begin to see and trust,
understanding that this matter cannot be transmitted, learned, calculated, or deliberated.
Since accompanying me south,
he has followed me by the desolate shores,
spending four years.
Once, when I brought up my late teacher's words for the Daoist Jishou—"It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing"—
he suddenly picked up a roasted bean by the stove and ate it.
From then on, even the exquisite offerings of fragrant feasts held no appeal for him,
except that steamed cakes and noodles were seldom without him—
he never missed a meal.
Now, as he comes to bid me farewell, temporarily returning to Zhejiang,
he brings this scroll seeking guidance,
and I offer him two verses in return.
Once Mǎzǔ asked Liàng the Lecturer:
"I hear you give great lectures on sūtras and śāstras - is this true?"
Liàng replied: "I dare not claim so."
Mǎzǔ asked again:
"Using what do you lecture?"
"Using the mind," he replied.
Mǎzǔ said:
"The mind is like an artisan,
consciousness like the assistant.
How could they possibly lecture on sūtras?"
Liàng said: "If the mind cannot lecture,
could it be that emptiness lectures instead?"
Mǎzǔ said:
"Indeed, it is emptiness that lectures."
Liàng remained unconvinced,
flicked his sleeves and started to leave.
Mǎzǔ then called out: "Lecturer!"
Liàng turned his head,
and suddenly experienced profound awakening.
He then bowed and departed,
directly entering Western Mountains,
with no further words to convey his realization.
Instantly cutting off the paths of ordinary and sage,
people nowadays seem to have it yet seem not to have it.
Some recognize only the teacher's verbal explanations,
thinking wheat contains flour, rice makes meal,
and thus seek understanding within wheat and rice.
They want the teacher to know they've grasped this principle,
fearing the teacher remains unaware.
Such people
only recognize what's before the donkey and behind the horse.
To wish to be like Liàng the Lecturer, who under Mǎzǔ's single word
immediately forgot his previous attainments -
is this not difficult indeed?
For Liàng was like pure steel forged, raw iron cast,
thus able to accomplish everything completely.
Immediately leaping beyond the profound subtleties of doctrinal teachings,
cutting off past and future,
with no dharma left to complete or not complete.
Nowadays lecturers, hearing the master say "emptiness lectures,"
immediately grope east and west within emptiness,
doubting if not slandering.
Dàomíng the Lecturer also expounded sūtras,
knowing that essential point certainly lies not in words or language.
Words and language are but fingers pointing at the moon.
Wishing to find a good teacher to understand this point
beyond verbal characteristics, beyond written signs, beyond mental conceptions,
he came seeking Miàoxǐ.
Miàoxǐ, moved by his sincerity,
directly wrote this gōng'àn for him.
Someday suddenly within written words
he'll recognize the message of special transmission outside teachings,
then know wheat contains no flour, meal isn't made from rice.
Knowing thus,
he'll be able before lecturing
to make a dead snake come alive and wriggling.
Say emptiness can lecture on sūtras,
emptiness cannot lecture on sūtras -
all are matters within one's own house.
No longer maintaining views of complete or incomplete
within or beyond teachings.
When dual views vanish,
lecturing time becomes non-lecturing time's,
non-lecturing time becomes lecturing time's.
Silent while speaking, speaking while silent,
the great gate of giving opens unobstructed.
True words, real words, such words,
neither deceptive nor false - such talk
greatly resembles dreaming without dreams,
urinating in bed with eyes open.
Those who write like this
deserve thirty strokes of the staff.
Although this is so,
using provisional names to guide sentient beings,
The ancient sage said:
The Way is not cultivated through artifice,
only avoid defilement.
This mountain monk says:
Speaking of mind and nature is defilement;
discussing mystery and wonder is defilement;
sitting in meditation and practicing concentration is defilement;
engaging in deliberate thought is defilement.
Even now, thus putting it into writing
is particularly defilement.
Beyond this,
after all, what is
the place of genuine attainment?
The vajra sword cuts directly overhead—
pay no mind to human judgments of right and wrong.
Zǒng Chán, just investigate thus.
Recently, while in Chángshā,
I received a letter from my teacher Yuánwù.
He mentioned that your late-life attainments through spiritual practice are truly extraordinary.
I have reflected on this repeatedly.
Eight years have now passed.
I have often regretted not having the opportunity to personally hear your remaining teachings.
My admiration for you only grows deeper.
Since my youth, I have resolved to seek enlightenment,
visiting wise teachers to inquire about this matter.
After reaching adulthood,
I became burdened by marriage and official duties,
unable to devote myself purely to practice.
Thus I procrastinated until now in old age,
still having gained no realization—a constant source of shame and sighing.
Nevertheless, my aspiration and vows
have never been confined to superficial understanding.
I believe that if enlightenment is not attained, so be it;
but if attained, it must reach the genuine realization of the ancient masters to be considered ultimate liberation.
Though my mind has never retreated for even a single thought,
I feel my practice remains ultimately impure.
This could be called great ambition with little strength.
Previously,
I earnestly implored Teacher Yuánwù,
who instructed me with six passages of Dharma words.
The first directly pointed to this matter,
followed by two kōans: Yúnmén’s "Lay it down" and Zhàozhōu’s "Mount Sumeru."
He urged this dull practitioner
to constantly reflect upon them,
assuring that prolonged effort would bring breakthrough.
Such was his compassionate guidance.
Yet my obstinate dullness remains overwhelming.
Now, fortunate to be free from worldly ties in private life,
residing idly without other concerns,
I am determined to vigorously discipline myself to fulfill my original aspiration.
My only regret is lacking your personal instruction.
All my lifelong shortcomings have been laid bare before you—
surely you can illuminate this mind of mine.
I implore your nuanced guidance and warnings:
How should I practice in daily life?
So that I may avoid straying onto other paths
and directly unite with the fundamental ground.
Such words as these
reveal no few shortcomings,
but since I sincerely offer myself, I cannot hide.
Truly deserving of compassion—
I reverently inquire.
I have received your letter and read it.
From your youth until entering official service, you have paid respects to many great masters.
In between, you were burdened by imperial examinations, marriage, and official duties.
Moreover, you were overcome by evil perceptions and habits.
You were unable to concentrate wholeheartedly on spiritual practice.
You consider this a grave offense.
Yet you are able to deeply reflect on the impermanence of this world and its various illusions, finding nothing truly joyful.
You single-mindedly wish to investigate this great matter of causation.
This greatly pleases this sick monk.
However, since you are a scholar-official who depends on salary for livelihood,
imperial examinations, marriage, and official duties
are unavoidable in worldly life.
These are not your fault.
To feel great fear over minor offenses
is only possible due to the profound conditioning from serving true spiritual friends and cultivating prajñā wisdom over countless great kalpas since beginningless time.
How else could it be so?
As for what you call grave offenses,
even sages and worthies cannot avoid them entirely.
But knowing they are illusory and not ultimate truth,
you can turn your mind to this path.
Using the water of prajñā wisdom,
wash away the filth of defilements.
Dwell in purity.
Cut them off decisively from under your feet.
Do not let continuous thoughts arise again—that is enough.
There is no need to dwell on the past or worry about the future.
Since they are illusory,
then acting is also illusion,
experiencing is also illusion,
perceiving is also illusion,
being deluded is also illusion.
Past, present, and future are all illusions.
Now that you recognize your errors,
use illusory medicine to cure illusory illness.
When the illness is healed, the medicine is discarded.
You remain the same person as before.
If you think there is another person or another method,
that is the view of heretics and demons.
Reflect on this deeply.
Just proceed along this cliff,
often in tranquil states,
but never forget the phrases "Place Mount Sumeru down" and "Start earnestly from under your feet."
Do not fear what has already passed,
nor dwell on it.
Dwelling and fearing will obstruct the path.
Simply before all buddhas,
make great vows,
wishing this mind to be firm,
never regressing or losing it.
Relying on the blessings of all buddhas,
encountering a true spiritual friend, under a single word,
instantly transcend life and death,
realize and certify unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
continue the wisdom life of the buddhas,
and repay the immense kindness of all buddhas.
If you practice like this, in time, there is no reason you will not awaken.
Consider how the youth Sudhana, starting from Mañjuśrī's inspiration,
gradually journeyed south through 110 cities,
visiting 53 spiritual friends.
Finally, in the snap of a finger before Maitreya,
he instantly forgot all the dharma gates attained from previous spiritual friends.
Again following Maitreya's teaching, he wished to see Mañjuśrī,
whereupon Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar,
reaching over 110 yojanas,
touched Sudhana's head, and said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Virtuous man,
if you lack the root of faith,
your mind is inferior, anxious, and regretful,
your practice is incomplete,
you regress and lose diligence,
cling to any good root,
are satisfied with little merit,
cannot skillfully arouse vows and practice,
are not protected by spiritual friends,
then you cannot fully understand such dharma nature,
such principles,
such dharma gates,
such practices,
such realms,
whether omniscient,
variously knowing,
exhausting the source,
comprehending,
entering,
expounding,
discriminating,
certifying,
or attaining,
all would be impossible."
Mañjuśrī thus instructed Sudhana,
and Sudhana instantly achieved asamkhyeya dharma gates,
possessed immeasurable great wisdom light,
entered Samantabhadra's gate,
and in one thought saw as many spiritual friends as dust motes in three thousand great thousand worlds,
intimately approaching all,
reverently serving them,
receiving and practicing their teachings,
attaining the wisdom of unforgetfulness,
the liberation of adornment treasury,
until entering Samantabhadra's pore-worlds,
taking one step in each pore,
passing unspeakable, unspeakable numbers of buddha-land dust-worlds,
equal to Samantabhadra,
equal to all buddhas,
equal in realms and practices,
and liberation and mastery all entirely equal,
without duality or distinction.
At such a time,
one can finally transform the three poisons into the three cumulative pure precepts,
transform the six consciousnesses into the six spiritual powers,
transform afflictions into bodhi,
transform ignorance into great wisdom.
The above series of teachings
depends solely on the individual's final true thought.
Sudhana, in the snap of Maitreya's finger,

are all real,

Since they are real,
then hell and heaven are also real,

then throughout the future,

Thinking that ancient virtuous ones

creating its own obstructions.
It has nothing to do with anything else.
You, sir, try working like this:
as days lengthen and months deepen,

just recite it like this,

If you are one with bone and sinew,

immediately take the Vajra King's precious sword

the path of ordinary and sage is cut off,
scheming pondering is cut off,
gain and loss, right and wrong are cut off.
Under the practitioner's very feet,

Is this not freeing?
Have you not heard?
In the past, when Venerable Guànxī first visited Línjì,

grabbed him by the chest.
Guànxī then said,
"I see, I see."
Línjì, knowing he had thoroughly penetrated,
immediately pushed him away.
There were no words or phrases to discuss with him.
At such a time,
how could Guànxī have managed by scheming pondering?
Fortunately, since ancient times there have been such examples.
But people nowadays do not take them seriously at all,
simply because they are coarse-minded.
If Guànxī back then had even a bit of a mind awaiting awakening, awaiting verification, awaiting rest placed upfront,
never mind being grabbed and then awakening—
even if you tied his hands and feet
and dragged him around the fourfold world,
he still would not attain awakening,
nor would he attain rest.
Ordinary scheming and arranging is consciousness.
That which flows along with birth and death is also consciousness.
Fear, panic, and anxiety are also consciousness.
Yet practitioners nowadays
do not know this is a sickness;
they just remain within it,
bobbing up and down.
As the teachings say: "Following consciousness, not following wisdom."
Thus, they obscure their original state and inherent face.
If one can momentarily put it all down,
not thinking or scheming at all,

then this very consciousness

There is no other wisdom to be attained.
If there is something else attained,
something else verified,
then it is not it.
It is like when one is lost, calling east west;
